track.title: Mind & Words
track.tagline: A random mind trick, bias or word every day, explained like you're 20

lessons.title: Confirmation bias
lessons.summary: Your brain loves being right, so it quietly hunts for proof you already are.

term.meaning: The habit of noticing, believing and remembering information that supports what you already think, and ignoring what doesn't.

sections.b: Imagine your brain has a bouncer at the door. Facts that agree with you walk straight in; facts that disagree get asked for ID and turned away. You don't feel this happening, it just feels like 'seeing the truth'. Everyone does it, smart people included, because being right feels safe and being wrong feels like a small threat.

Rohan decides in week one that his new teammate Ankit is lazy. Now every time Ankit logs off at 6 pm, Rohan notices. The three times Ankit fixed a production bug at midnight? Rohan barely registers them. In the family WhatsApp group, Mausi forwards only articles that 'prove' her favourite home remedy works, and every forward feels like more evidence.

• You only Google phrases that already contain your answer (“why X is bad”)
• Evidence against your view makes you irritated instead of curious
• You remember the hits and forget the misses
• Your feed shows only people who agree with you

• Ask yourself: “What would change my mind?” If the answer is “nothing”, that's a red flag
• Search for the opposite view on purpose: “arguments for X” and “arguments against X”
• Before judging a colleague, list 2 facts that don't fit your story about them
• Invite one person who usually disagrees with you to poke holes in your plan

lessons.action: Pick one strong opinion you hold and spend 5 minutes reading the best argument against it.

quiz.q: What is confirmation bias?
options: Favouring information that supports what you already believe
quiz.why: It's the brain filtering for agreement and filtering out disagreement.

quiz.q: Your manager already thinks a project will fail and only brings up its problems in every meeting, ignoring the good numbers. Which is this?
quiz.why: She's selectively noticing evidence that fits her existing belief.

quiz.q: Which question best fights confirmation bias?
options: How can I prove I'm right?
What evidence would change my mind?
What did I believe last year?
quiz.why: Actively looking for disconfirming evidence breaks the filter.

lessons.title: Anchoring bias
lessons.summary: The first number you hear sticks like chewing gum and drags every later guess towards it.

term.meaning: Relying too heavily on the first piece of information you get (the 'anchor') when making decisions.

sections.b: Think of a boat dropping an anchor: it can drift a bit, but never far from where the anchor landed. Your brain does the same with the first number or idea it hears. Even a random or silly first number pulls your estimate towards it. Shops, salary negotiators and sellers know this very well.

Priya sees a kurta tagged ₹4,999, slashed to ₹1,999. It feels like a steal, but she'd never have paid ₹1,999 if the tag had just said ₹1,999. In a job offer call, HR asks Arjun, “What's your current CTC?” first, and the whole negotiation now orbits that number instead of what the role is actually worth in the market.

• A 'was ₹X, now ₹Y' price makes you feel you're winning
• The first offer in a negotiation sets the range for the whole talk
• You judge an estimate as 'reasonable' just because it's lower than a crazy first guess
• Your opinion of someone is stuck on a first impression

• Research the real market value before you see anyone's number
• In salary talks, try to share your researched expected range first, so your anchor sets the tone
• Ask: “Would I still pay this if I'd never seen the original price?”
• When you hear an anchor, consciously come up with your own number from scratch

lessons.action: Next time you see a 'discount', ask yourself what you'd pay if there was no crossed-out price.

quiz.q: What does anchoring mean?
options: Over-relying on the first piece of information you get
quiz.why: The first number or fact becomes a reference point that drags later judgments.

quiz.q: A car dealer starts at ₹12 lakh, then 'generously' drops to ₹9.5 lakh, which still feels like a bargain even though similar cars sell for ₹8.5 lakh. Which is this?
quiz.why: The high first price became the anchor that made ₹9.5 lakh feel cheap.

quiz.q: Best defence against anchoring in a salary negotiation?
options: Know the market range beforehand and state your own number
Accept the first offer to look polite
Ask friends to guess a number
quiz.why: Independent research gives you your own anchor.

lessons.title: Sunk cost fallacy
lessons.summary: 'But I've already put so much in!' is how good people stay stuck in bad deals.

term.meaning: Continuing something because of what you've already invested (time, money, effort), even when continuing no longer makes sense.

sections.b: Money or time you've already spent is gone, whatever you do next. But your brain hates 'wasting' it, so it pushes you to keep going to 'make it worth it'. It's like staying in a boring movie because you paid for the ticket, now you've lost the ticket money AND two hours. Good decisions look forward, not backward.

Sneha has spent 2 years and ₹3 lakh preparing for an exam she no longer wants to clear, but quitting feels like 'throwing it all away'. At work, a team keeps pouring months into a product nobody uses because 'we've already built 80% of it'. Even finishing a terrible ₹600 Swiggy biryani 'because I paid for it' is a tiny sunk cost moment.

• Your main reason to continue is “I've already invested so much”
• You'd never start this today, yet you won't stop it
• You feel quitting = admitting you were wrong
• More effort keeps going in without the results improving

• Ask: “If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?”
• Separate the past cost from the future benefit: only the future is still in your control
• Set a checkpoint in advance (“If no traction by March, we stop”)
• Reframe quitting as saving your future time, not wasting your past

lessons.action: Think of one thing you're continuing mainly because of what you've already spent, and ask the 'fresh start' question.

quiz.q: Sunk cost fallacy is…
options: Spending too little on something important
Continuing something because of past investment, not future value
Believing a losing streak must end
quiz.why: Past costs are gone; they shouldn't decide the future.

quiz.q: Your friend stays in a course he hates because 'I've already paid the full fees'. Which is this?
quiz.why: The money is spent either way; staying only adds more lost time.

quiz.q: Which question best counters sunk cost thinking?
options: What will people say if I quit?
How much have I already spent?
If I were starting today, would I choose this?
quiz.why: It forces a forward-looking decision.

lessons.title: Availability heuristic
lessons.summary: If it comes to mind easily, your brain assumes it must be common.

term.meaning: Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples pop into your head.

sections.b: Your brain uses a shortcut: 'Can I quickly remember an example? Then it must happen a lot.' The problem is that dramatic, recent or emotional stories are easier to remember, not more common. News of one plane crash sticks; thousands of boring safe flights don't. So your sense of risk gets bent by what's vivid.

After watching three reels about people losing money in stock market scams, Karan decides all investing is a scam and keeps everything in a savings account. Meanwhile he happily drives without a seatbelt in the back seat, which is statistically a much bigger risk but never shows up in his feed.

• Your fear of something spikes right after a news story or viral video
• You say “everyone” or “always” based on 2-3 memorable cases
• Rare dramatic risks worry you more than common boring ones
• One bad experience defines a whole category (one rude auto driver = all auto drivers)

• Ask: “Is this common, or just memorable?”
• Look for actual numbers or base rates before deciding
• Notice when your feed is shaping your sense of danger
• Balance one vivid story with a quick check of the bigger picture

lessons.action: Notice one fear or belief today that came from a viral story rather than actual data.

quiz.q: The availability heuristic means…
options: Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind
Trusting what is available in shops
quiz.why: Easy-to-recall examples feel more frequent than they are.

quiz.q: After a colleague's laptop gets hacked, your team suddenly believes hacking is the company's biggest risk, though data loss from bad backups is far more common. Which is this?
quiz.why: A vivid recent event inflated the perceived risk.

quiz.q: Best counter-move?
options: Check real numbers or base rates
Watch more videos on the topic
quiz.why: Data corrects the distortion of memorable stories.

lessons.title: Dunning–Kruger effect
lessons.summary: Knowing a little can feel like knowing a lot, until you learn more.

term.meaning: The idea that people with low skill in an area tend to overestimate their ability, while skilled people may underestimate theirs.

sections.b: When you've watched two YouTube videos on cooking, you don't yet know how much you don't know, so you feel confident. As you learn more, you see how big the field is and your confidence often dips. Quick honesty note: the original 1999 study is real, but the popular 'Mount Stupid' meme exaggerates it, and researchers still debate how much is a true effect versus a statistical artefact. Treat it as a useful reminder, not a law of nature.

Vikram reads one thread on crypto and starts confidently advising the whole family group on where to invest. Meanwhile, his cousin Meera, a chartered accountant, keeps saying “it depends” and “I'd need to check”, because she knows how many factors matter. Guess who sounds more sure?

• Very confident opinions after very little learning (yours or others')
• Someone dismisses experts with “it's not that complicated”
• No questions asked, only answers given
• Real experts in the room sound more cautious than beginners

• Ask yourself: “How would I rate my knowledge out of 10, and what's my evidence?”
• Seek feedback from people who are clearly better than you
• Treat confident beginners kindly but check their claims
• If you're new to something, say “I'm still learning this” out loud; it's a strength

lessons.action: Pick one topic you feel strongly about and list three things about it you genuinely don't know.

quiz.q: What does the popular version of the Dunning–Kruger effect claim?
options: Low-skill people often overestimate their ability
quiz.why: That's the popular summary, though the size of the effect is debated.

quiz.q: Your new intern, after one week, insists the senior architect's design is 'obviously wrong' without understanding the constraints. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Limited knowledge can hide how much you don't know.

quiz.q: Which statement about Dunning–Kruger is most accurate?
options: It's a real finding, but the popular meme exaggerates it and it's debated
It was invented by social media
It means experts are always wrong
It's proven to apply to every person in every skill
quiz.why: Researchers still argue about how much is statistical artefact.

lessons.title: Negativity bias
lessons.summary: One criticism can outweigh ten compliments in your head. Here's why.

term.meaning: The tendency for negative experiences, comments and news to affect us more strongly than equally sized positive ones.

sections.b: For our ancestors, missing a tiger was deadly while missing a nice sunset was no big deal. So brains learned to treat bad stuff as more urgent. Today that means one sharp comment from your boss can ruin a whole good day. It's normal wiring, but it can make life feel worse than it actually is.

Ananya's performance review has nine strengths and one 'area to improve'. She replays that one line all weekend. On Instagram, 200 kind comments on her post feel like nothing next to the single rude one. Her dad watches the evening news and becomes convinced the world is falling apart.

• You remember the one bad comment, not the many good ones
• A small setback makes the whole day feel 'ruined'
• You expect the worst outcome by default
• Doom-scrolling news leaves you anxious but not better informed

• Write down 3 good things that happened today, on purpose
• When you get feedback, re-read the positives slowly, too
• Ask: “Is this one thing really bigger than everything else, or just louder?”
• Limit news and comment sections, especially before bed

lessons.action: Tonight, write down three small good moments from your day.

quiz.q: Negativity bias means…
options: Bad things affect us more strongly than equally good things
quiz.why: Our brains give extra weight to negative information.

quiz.q: You get 15 'great job' messages and one 'this slide is confusing', and you can't stop thinking about the slide. Which is this?
quiz.why: The single negative outweighs many positives.

quiz.q: Which habit helps balance negativity bias?
quiz.why: It trains attention towards positives too.

lessons.title: Fundamental attribution error
lessons.summary: When others mess up, it's their character. When you mess up, it's the traffic.

term.meaning: Blaming other people's behaviour on their personality while underestimating the situation they were in.

sections.b: If someone cuts you off on the road, your brain shouts 'What an idiot!' If you cut someone off, you think 'I was late, the signal was confusing'. We see our own situation clearly but only see other people's actions. So we judge them as people, not as humans having a bad day.

Neha's teammate Rahul misses a deadline and Neha thinks, “He's so careless.” Later she finds out his father was hospitalised that week. In a family function, an aunt decides the new bahu is 'rude' because she didn't smile much, without knowing she had a migraine and had travelled overnight.

• You use labels like lazy, rude, selfish after one incident
• You don't ask what was happening for them
• Your own mistakes always have reasons; theirs never do
• Your judgment changes completely once you hear the backstory

• Ask: “What situation could make a decent person act like this?”
• Before labelling, ask a gentle question (“Everything okay this week?”)
• Give others the same excuses you give yourself
• Separate the behaviour (“the report was late”) from the person (“he's useless”)

lessons.action: The next time someone annoys you today, think of one situational reason they might have acted that way.

quiz.q: The fundamental attribution error is…
options: Blaming others' actions on character, not circumstances
quiz.why: We overlook situational factors for other people.

quiz.q: A delivery guy is late and you decide he's 'irresponsible', but there was a huge jam due to rain. Which is this?
quiz.why: You blamed his character instead of the situation.

quiz.q: What's a good counter-move?
options: Ask what situation might explain the behaviour
Assume the worst to stay safe
quiz.why: Considering context reduces unfair judgments.

lessons.title: Hindsight bias
lessons.summary: 'I knew it all along!' Mostly, you didn't.

term.meaning: The feeling, after something happens, that you could have easily predicted it.

sections.b: Once you know the ending of a movie, all the clues look obvious. Real life works the same: after the result is out, your brain rewrites history so the outcome feels like it was always clear. This makes us judge past decisions (ours and others') too harshly and learn the wrong lessons.

After India loses a match, Uncle in the WhatsApp group says, “I told you, they should never have batted first,” though he said nothing before the toss. At work, after a launch flops, people say the problems were 'obvious', even though everyone approved the plan in the meeting.

• “I knew it!” said only after the result
• Harsh judgment of decisions made with less information
• Post-mortems that blame people for not seeing the future
• Feeling stupid about past choices that were reasonable at the time

• Write down predictions before big events, then compare honestly
• Judge decisions by the information available then, not now
• In reviews, ask “What did we know at the time?”
• Be kind to your past self; he or she didn't have today's knowledge

lessons.action: Write down one prediction for this week (a match, a meeting outcome) and check it later.

quiz.q: Hindsight bias is…
options: Believing after the fact that an outcome was predictable
quiz.why: Knowing the result makes it feel obvious in retrospect.

quiz.q: After a stock crashes, your friend says 'it was obvious', but last month he was recommending it. Which is this?
quiz.why: He's rewriting what he 'knew' after seeing the outcome.

quiz.q: A good way to reduce hindsight bias?
quiz.why: A written record shows what you actually expected.

lessons.title: Optimism bias & planning fallacy
lessons.summary: 'This will take 2 days.' Narrator: it took 2 weeks.

term.meaning: Underestimating how long, how costly or how hard a task will be, even when similar tasks took longer before.

sections.b: Your brain imagines the best-case version of a plan, where nothing goes wrong. It forgets about sick days, bugs, meetings and that one person who replies late. Optimism bias is the broader belief that bad things are less likely to happen to you than to others. A little optimism is healthy; planning only on it is not.

Aditya promises his manager the feature will be ready by Friday. He doesn't account for the code review, the client's change request, or the Diwali week. A couple planning a wedding budget of ₹8 lakh ends up at ₹14 lakh, like almost every relative before them.

• Your estimates assume everything goes smoothly
• You keep missing your own deadlines but estimate the same way
• “It won't happen to me” about risks like health or job loss
• No buffer in plans or budgets

• Look at how long similar tasks actually took last time, and use that
• Add a buffer (many people use 1.5x time and 1.2x budget)
• Break tasks into small steps and estimate each
• Ask a colleague: “What could go wrong here?”

lessons.action: Take one task on today's list and estimate its time, then note how long it really took.

quiz.q: The planning fallacy is…
options: Underestimating time and cost even when past tasks took longer
quiz.why: We plan for the best case and ignore history.

quiz.q: Your team says a migration will take 1 sprint; the last three migrations each took 3 sprints. Which bias is at play?
quiz.why: They're ignoring the track record of similar tasks.

quiz.q: Best practical fix?
options: Base estimates on how long similar tasks actually took
Let the most confident person decide
quiz.why: Past data is more reliable than imagination.

lessons.title: Bandwagon effect
lessons.summary: If everyone's doing it, it must be right… right?

term.meaning: Adopting a belief or behaviour mainly because many other people are doing it.

sections.b: Humans are social animals: for most of history, going with the group kept you safe. So when lots of people like something, your brain treats popularity as proof. That's why queues attract more people and 'trending' tags work. Sometimes the crowd is right, but popularity alone isn't evidence.

Everyone in Siddharth's office is buying a certain small-cap stock after a 'tip' in a Telegram group, so he buys too without checking the company. On Instagram, a café with a 1-hour queue looks amazing simply because of the queue. In meetings, once two seniors agree, everyone else nods along.

• Your main reason is “everyone's doing it”
• FOMO pushes you to act fast
• Trending, bestseller or 'most booked' labels sway you
• You change your opinion after seeing which side is bigger

• Ask: “Would I still want this if nobody else did?”
• Do your own 10-minute check before following a trend
• In meetings, write your view down before hearing others
• Remember: crowds can be wrong (think of past investment bubbles)

lessons.action: Notice one thing today you're tempted to do just because it's trending.

quiz.q: The bandwagon effect means…
options: Doing something mainly because many others do
quiz.why: Popularity is treated as proof.

quiz.q: Your whole friend group starts a new ₹3,000/month app subscription, and you sign up without knowing what it does. Which is this?
quiz.why: You joined because others did.

quiz.q: Which question helps resist the bandwagon?
options: Would I want this if nobody else did?
Who's the most popular person using it?
quiz.why: It separates your judgment from the crowd's.

lessons.title: Loss aversion
lessons.summary: Losing ₹500 hurts more than finding ₹500 feels good.

term.meaning: The tendency to feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size, so we work harder to avoid losing than to win.

sections.b: Imagine finding a ₹500 note: nice. Now imagine losing one: that stings much more. Research suggests losses often feel roughly twice as strong as equal gains, though the exact size varies. This makes us cling to things, avoid smart risks and fall for 'don't miss out' marketing.

Pooja's shares are down 30%. She won't sell and move the money to a better option because selling would 'make the loss real'. Apps say “Your cart items are about to expire!” and suddenly you buy stuff you didn't need. An employee stays in a bad job because leaving means 'losing' the bonus due in 8 months.

• You hold onto losing investments hoping to 'break even'
• 'Last chance' and 'offer ends tonight' push you to act
• You avoid good opportunities because of a small risk
• Free trials turn into paid subscriptions because cancelling feels like losing something

• Ask: “If I didn't already own this, would I buy it today?”
• Look at total outcomes, not just the scary loss part
• Ignore countdown timers; real deals come back
• Set rules in advance (e.g. review investments every 6 months, not daily)

lessons.action: Spot one 'limited time' or 'don't lose this' message today and ask if you'd want it without the pressure.

quiz.q: Loss aversion means…
options: Losses feel stronger than equal gains
quiz.why: A loss hurts more than a same-sized gain pleases.

quiz.q: A shopping app shows 'You'll lose your ₹200 coupon in 2 hours!' and you buy something you didn't plan to. Which is this using?
quiz.why: Fear of losing the coupon drove the purchase.

quiz.q: Which question best counters loss aversion with investments?
options: How much have I lost so far?
If I didn't own this, would I buy it today?
quiz.why: It shifts focus to the future value.

lessons.title: Status quo bias
lessons.summary: Changing things feels risky, so we stick with 'how it's always been'.

term.meaning: Preferring things to stay the same, even when a change would be better for us.

sections.b: The current situation feels safe because you know it, even if it's not great. Change means effort, uncertainty and possible regret. So your brain makes 'do nothing' the default winner. That's why companies make auto-renewal the default: most people never switch.

Kunal has had the same bank account and insurance policy for 10 years, paying high fees, because switching feels like hassle. His team still uses a messy Excel tracker because 'that's how we've always done it', even though a free tool would save hours. His parents keep money in a low-interest FD for years without comparing.

• “We've always done it this way” is the main argument
• You keep default settings and plans without checking
• You postpone decisions until they make themselves
• Even small improvements feel like too much effort

• Pretend you're choosing from zero: which option would you pick today?
• Put one 'review day' a year on your calendar for subscriptions, insurance, plans
• Make change smaller: try the new option for one week
• Ask: “What is staying the same costing me?”

lessons.action: Check one subscription or default setting today and decide if you'd choose it again.

quiz.q: Status quo bias is…
options: Preferring things stay the same even when change is better
quiz.why: The current state feels safe by default.

quiz.q: Your company keeps a slow approval process 'because it's always been this way', though everyone hates it. Which is this?
quiz.why: The existing way wins just because it exists.

quiz.q: Why do companies make subscriptions auto-renew by default?
options: Most people stick with the default
quiz.why: They're using status quo bias.

lessons.title: Framing effect
lessons.summary: Same facts, different wrapping, totally different decision.

term.meaning: Reacting differently to the same information depending on how it's presented.

sections.b: '90% fat-free' sounds healthy; '10% fat' sounds greasy. They're the same thing. Your brain reacts to the wrapping paper, not just the gift inside. Marketers, politicians and even your manager use framing to steer how you feel.

A doctor tells Riya's dad a surgery has a '90% survival rate' and he agrees. Another doctor says '10% of patients die' and he panics. Same numbers. At work, a manager says “We're giving you the opportunity to lead this extra project” instead of “We need you to do more work for the same pay.”

• A positive or negative spin changes how you feel about the same fact
• Percentages that sound good but hide the other side
• 'Opportunity' language for extra unpaid work
• Ads that compare to the worst option to make theirs look great

• Flip the frame: restate it the other way (90% success = 10% failure)
• Ask for the raw numbers, not just the summary
• Ask: “What exactly changes for me?” when something is framed as an opportunity
• Sleep on decisions that feel urgent because of the wording

lessons.action: When you see a statistic today, restate it in the opposite frame and see if your feeling changes.

quiz.q: The framing effect is…
options: Reacting differently to the same info depending on how it's presented
quiz.why: Wording changes perception even when facts are identical.

quiz.q: Your boss calls weekend work 'a great chance to show leadership'. Which is mainly at play?
quiz.why: The same request is wrapped in a positive frame.

quiz.q: Which tip counters framing?
options: Restate the information in the opposite frame
quiz.why: Flipping the frame reveals the full picture.

lessons.title: Survivorship bias
lessons.summary: You only hear from the winners. The losers don't give TED talks.

term.meaning: Drawing conclusions only from the people or things that 'survived' or succeeded, while ignoring the many that failed.

sections.b: We hear about the college dropout who became a billionaire, not the thousands of dropouts who struggled. So we think 'dropping out works'. It's like judging a lottery only by interviewing winners. The failures are invisible, so the picture is badly lopsided.

Rohit sees LinkedIn posts from people who quit their jobs to become full-time influencers and decides to do the same. He doesn't see the hundreds who tried, ran out of savings and quietly went back to jobs. Old buildings seem 'better made than today', but that's partly because the badly made ones already fell down.

• Advice based only on success stories
• “He did it, so anyone can” arguments
• No mention of how many tried and failed
• 'They don't make them like they used to' style thinking

• Ask: “Who tried this and failed, and why don't I hear about them?”
• Look for the full numbers (how many startups fail in 5 years?)
• Learn from failures, not just from winners
• Treat 'success secrets' as one data point, not a formula

lessons.action: When you see a success story today, ask what the failure rate is for people who tried the same thing.

quiz.q: Survivorship bias means…
options: Focusing on successes while ignoring the failures you don't see
quiz.why: Invisible failures distort the picture.

quiz.q: Your cousin says 'All successful founders dropped out, so you should too'. Which bias is he showing?
quiz.why: He ignores the many dropouts who didn't succeed.

quiz.q: Best question to ask?
options: How many tried this and failed?
Who is the most famous success?
What brand does the winner use?
quiz.why: It brings the hidden failures into view.

lessons.title: Recency bias
lessons.summary: What happened last week can shout louder than what happened all year.

term.meaning: Giving more weight to recent events than to older ones, even when the older ones matter just as much.

sections.b: Your memory is like a phone gallery: the newest photos are at the top and easiest to see. So recent events feel more important. In performance reviews, this is a big deal: a manager may remember your last month far better than your first ten. In investing, people assume the latest trend will continue forever.

Shruti delivered brilliant work from April to January, then had one messy project in February. Her March appraisal focuses almost entirely on February. Meanwhile, Varun did little all year but shone in the last month and gets a glowing review. Investors pile into whatever fund did best last quarter.

• Reviews mainly mention the last few weeks
• You judge a person or team by their latest result only
• Assuming a recent trend (market, cricket form) will continue
• Forgetting older wins when something recently went wrong

• Keep a 'brag document': note wins monthly so you can share them at review time
• If you're a manager, keep notes on each person through the year
• Look at long-term data (5-year returns, not last 3 months)
• Ask: “Is this recent event typical or unusual?”

lessons.action: Start a simple note today listing one work win from this month.

quiz.q: Recency bias is…
options: Overweighting recent events compared to older ones
quiz.why: Recent events are easier to recall and feel bigger.

quiz.q: Your manager rates you poorly based only on one bad month, ignoring a strong year. Which bias is this?
quiz.why: The latest month dominated the whole review.

quiz.q: Which habit protects you from recency bias in appraisals?
options: Keep a running log of your achievements
Work hardest only in the last month
quiz.why: A record brings older wins back into view.

lessons.title: In-group bias
lessons.summary: 'My people' feel more trustworthy, even when they aren't.

term.meaning: Favouring people who belong to your own group (team, city, college, community) over outsiders.

sections.b: Your brain quickly sorts people into 'us' and 'them'. Then it gives 'us' more trust, kindness and benefit of the doubt. It even happens with silly, random groups in experiments. It feels like loyalty, but it can quietly become unfair.

In a hiring panel, Manish gives a higher rating to the candidate from his own college, even though another candidate answered better. In the society WhatsApp group, a mistake by a long-time resident is forgiven but the same mistake by a new tenant is 'typical'. Fans of rival IPL teams judge the same umpiring decision completely differently.

• You trust someone more because of shared college, language, city or community
• The same behaviour feels okay from 'us' and wrong from 'them'
• Jokes or stereotypes about outsiders feel harmless
• Teams protect their own members even when they're wrong

• Ask: “Would I judge this the same way if it was someone from another group?”
• Use clear criteria (scorecards) in hiring and reviews
• Make friends and contacts outside your usual circles
• Notice 'us vs them' language in yourself and others

lessons.action: Notice one moment today where you trusted or judged someone mainly because of which 'group' they belong to.

quiz.q: In-group bias means…
options: Favouring people from your own group
quiz.why: We give 'us' more benefit of the doubt than 'them'.

quiz.q: Your team lead always gives the best projects to people from his hometown. Which is this most likely?
quiz.why: He's favouring his own group.

quiz.q: A good fix in hiring?
options: Use the same clear scorecard for every candidate
quiz.why: Structured criteria reduce favouritism.

lessons.title: Self-serving bias
lessons.summary: Wins are thanks to me. Losses are thanks to… literally anything else.

term.meaning: Taking credit for successes but blaming outside factors for failures.

sections.b: When you top an exam, it's because you're smart and hardworking. When you fail, the paper was unfair. Your brain does this to protect your self-esteem, which isn't all bad. But if you never own your failures, you never learn from them.

When Amit's sales numbers are great, he says it's his pitch skills. When they drop, it's 'the market', 'the product team' or 'bad leads'. In a relationship, Kavya thinks fights happen because her partner is moody, but good days are because she's patient.

• Success stories always star you; failure stories star someone else
• You get defensive when asked what you could have done differently
• Team wins are 'mine', team losses are 'theirs'
• You never say “that was my mistake”

• After any outcome, ask: “What part was me, what part was luck or others?”
• Practise saying “I got that wrong, here's what I'll change”
• Give credit to others in wins, publicly
• Ask a trusted friend for honest feedback

lessons.action: Think of one recent failure and name one thing that was genuinely in your control.

quiz.q: Self-serving bias is…
options: Crediting yourself for success, blaming others for failure
quiz.why: It protects self-esteem but blocks learning.

quiz.q: A colleague says 'I closed this deal' when it wins, and 'marketing failed us' when it's lost. Which is this?
quiz.why: Credit inward, blame outward.

quiz.q: Best counter-move?
options: Ask what part of the outcome was in your control
quiz.why: Balanced reflection allows learning.

lessons.title: Choice overload
lessons.summary: More options should make us happier. Often they just make us stuck.

term.meaning: When too many options make decisions harder, slower and less satisfying.

sections.b: Picking between 3 dosas is easy. Picking between 47 OTT shows takes so long you end up rewatching an old one. Too many choices tire your brain, and afterwards you keep wondering if another option was better. Research on this is mixed, it doesn't happen every time, but it's very common when options are many and similar.

Megha spends 45 minutes scrolling Swiggy and orders the same paneer roll as always. Nikhil compares 30 phones for three weeks, finally buys one and still feels he made the wrong pick. HR gives employees 20 investment fund options and many simply don't choose at all.

• Endless scrolling, comparing and tab-opening
• Decision fatigue: you feel tired before you even choose
• You postpone or pick the default
• Regret afterwards, wondering about the other options

• Limit yourself to 3 options before comparing in detail
• Decide your 2-3 must-have criteria first
• Set a time limit (“I'll choose in 10 minutes”)
• Aim for 'good enough' instead of 'perfect' for small decisions

lessons.action: Next time you order food or pick a show, give yourself a 3-minute limit.

quiz.q: Choice overload means…
options: Too many options make deciding harder and less satisfying
quiz.why: Lots of similar options can cause stress and regret.

quiz.q: Your friend spends 2 hours comparing 40 hotels and books none. Which is this?
quiz.why: Too many options led to paralysis.

quiz.q: Which tip helps most?
options: Narrow to 3 options using must-have criteria
quiz.why: Fewer, filtered options make decisions easier.

lessons.title: Authority bias
lessons.summary: A white coat, a big title or a blue tick can switch off our thinking.

term.meaning: Giving too much weight to the opinion of someone who seems to be an authority, even outside their area or when they're wrong.

sections.b: From childhood we're taught to listen to parents, teachers and bosses, and often that's sensible. But the brain overgeneralises: anyone who looks or sounds like an authority gets automatic trust. Scammers know this, so they pretend to be police, bank officials or 'doctors' on YouTube.

Ravi's father gets a call from someone claiming to be from the 'cyber crime department', demanding a fine. The confident tone and official words almost make him pay. At work, nobody questions the VP's clearly flawed plan because she's the VP. A famous cricketer endorses a gaming app and fans assume it's safe.

• You accept a claim because of who said it, not the evidence
• Titles, uniforms or verified badges make you stop questioning
• Experts speaking outside their field (actor giving medical advice)
• Pressure to act urgently because 'an official' said so

• Ask: “Is this person an expert in THIS specific topic?”
• Verify independently: call the bank or police using the official number yourself
• In meetings, ask respectful questions: “Can you help me understand the data behind this?”
• Remember: real officials don't demand instant payments over calls

lessons.action: Notice one claim today you believed mainly because of who said it, and check the evidence.

quiz.q: Authority bias is…
options: Over-trusting people who seem to be authorities
quiz.why: Titles and status can override our own judgment.

quiz.q: A caller says he's from 'RBI' and asks your mother to share an OTP to 'protect her account'. Which bias is he exploiting?
quiz.why: He uses an official-sounding identity to get compliance.

quiz.q: Good counter-move?
options: Verify via an official number you find yourself
Trust them if they sound confident
Ask the caller for their number
quiz.why: Independent verification breaks the spell.

lessons.title: Gambler's fallacy
lessons.summary: 'It's been tails five times, so heads is due!' The coin doesn't remember.

term.meaning: Believing that past random events change the odds of future random events, like a 'due' win after many losses.

sections.b: A fair coin has no memory. Each toss is 50-50, no matter what happened before. But our brains love patterns and believe things 'balance out' in the short term. That's how people keep betting, or keep buying lottery tickets, sure their luck must turn.

Deepak loses five times in a row on a fantasy cricket app and thinks, “My win is due now,” so he bets bigger. A couple with three daughters is told by relatives that 'the next one will surely be a boy'. A trader assumes a stock that fell for 7 days 'has to' go up tomorrow.

• Thoughts like “I'm due for a win” or “It can't happen again”
• Increasing bets after losses to 'win it back'
• Seeing patterns in random events
• Confusing truly random events with ones that have real causes

• Remind yourself: random events have no memory
• Set a fixed money and time limit before playing any game
• Never chase losses; stop when you hit your limit
• If betting or gaming feels out of control, talk to someone you trust or a counsellor

lessons.action: Next time you hear 'it's due', ask: is this actually random, and if so, have the odds really changed?

quiz.q: The gambler's fallacy is…
options: Believing past random results change future odds
quiz.why: Independent random events don't 'balance out' on demand.

quiz.q: Your friend lost 6 fantasy contests and says, 'The next one is surely mine, I'll double my entry.' Which is this?
quiz.why: He thinks a win is 'due' after losses.

quiz.q: What's the probability of heads after 5 tails on a fair coin?
quiz.why: Each toss is independent.

lessons.title: Gaslighting
lessons.summary: When someone keeps making you doubt your own memory, you're not 'going crazy'.

term.meaning: A pattern where someone repeatedly denies, twists or rewrites what happened so you start doubting your own memory, perception or sanity.

sections.b: Imagine you clearly remember someone saying something, and they flatly say “I never said that, you're imagining things.” Once is a disagreement. Over and over, until you start trusting their version over your own mind, is gaslighting. Note: everyone misremembers sometimes, and honest disagreements happen; gaslighting is a repeated pattern that leaves you confused and dependent. This is a popular-psychology description of behaviour, not a label to diagnose anyone with.

In a meeting, Tanvi's manager agreed to a deadline extension. Next week he says, “I never agreed to that, you always twist my words. Are you sure you're managing your stress?” In a relationship, Arjun's partner says “You're too sensitive, that's not what happened” every time he brings up a hurtful comment, until he stops trusting himself.

• “That never happened” or “You're imagining it” about things you clearly remember
• You often feel confused, apologise a lot and second-guess yourself
• Your feelings are labelled 'too sensitive' or 'crazy'
• You start keeping notes just to prove to yourself what happened

• Write things down: dates, what was said, emails, screenshots
• Confirm important agreements in writing (“As discussed, the deadline is now 20th”)
• Calm script: “I remember it differently. Let's put it in writing going forward.”
• Reality-check with a trusted friend or a counsellor; if you feel unsafe or overwhelmed, call Tele-MANAS on 14416

lessons.action: After any important verbal agreement today, send a short 'as discussed' message to confirm it.

quiz.q: What best describes gaslighting?
options: Repeatedly making someone doubt their own memory or perception
quiz.why: It's a repeated pattern of denying and rewriting reality.

quiz.q: Your colleague keeps saying 'I never told you that' about tasks he assigned on calls, and suggests you have memory problems. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Repeated denial plus making you doubt your mind fits gaslighting.

quiz.q: Most useful first protection?
options: Agree with their version to keep peace
Document conversations and confirm agreements in writing
quiz.why: A written record protects your reality without needing to win arguments.

lessons.title: Covert (vulnerable) narcissism
lessons.summary: Not every self-centred person is loud. Some are quiet, wounded and hard to spot.

term.meaning: A popular term for a quieter style of self-centredness: hidden entitlement and need for admiration showing up as sulking, victimhood and passive-aggression rather than bragging.

sections.b: When people think 'narcissist', they picture someone loud and arrogant. The 'covert' or 'vulnerable' style looks different: shy, easily hurt, always feeling unappreciated, quietly resentful when they don't get special treatment. Important: only a qualified professional can diagnose Narcissistic Personality Disorder. Everyone has some of these traits on a bad day. Use this idea to understand behaviour and protect yourself, not to label people.

Rahul's friend Sameer never brags, but every conversation drifts to how life has been unfair to him. When Rahul shares his promotion, Sameer goes quiet, then says, “Must be nice when things just fall into your lap.” If Rahul can't attend his birthday, Sameer sulks for weeks and tells others Rahul 'never cared'.

• Constant sense of being misunderstood or unappreciated
• Your good news is met with coldness, sulking or subtle digs
• Passive-aggressive comments instead of direct asks
• Criticism of them, however gentle, leads to deep hurt or silent anger

• Don't try to diagnose; focus on the specific behaviour and how it affects you
• Keep your good news and vulnerable details for people who celebrate you
• Calm script: “I hear you're upset. I'm happy to talk when we can both be calm.”
• Set limits on time and emotional labour; talk to a counsellor if it's draining you

lessons.action: Notice who in your life genuinely celebrates your wins, and who goes quiet.

quiz.q: How is 'covert narcissism' usually described in popular psychology?
options: Quiet entitlement shown through sulking, victimhood and passive-aggression
quiz.why: It's a quieter style, not simply shyness.

quiz.q: Who can diagnose Narcissistic Personality Disorder?
options: Anyone who has read about it
quiz.why: Labels from articles are not diagnoses.

quiz.q: A friend meets every piece of your good news with a cold 'Lucky you, some of us actually struggle.' What's a healthy response?
options: Share wins with supportive people and set limits with this friend
quiz.why: Focus on boundaries, not labels.

lessons.title: Triangulation
lessons.summary: When someone drags a third person into your relationship to control you.

term.meaning: Bringing a third person into a conflict or relationship, directly or by comparison, to create jealousy, competition or pressure.

sections.b: Instead of talking to you directly, the person uses someone else as a tool. 'Your sister would never do this.' 'My ex used to understand me.' Or they pass messages through others so you never get a clear, direct conversation. It keeps you insecure and competing for approval. People do this unconsciously sometimes; it's the repeated pattern that matters.

In a joint family, a mother-in-law tells her son, “Your bhabhi always touches my feet, I don't know why your wife can't.” Now the two women compete. At work, a manager tells Riya, “Karthik finishes this in half the time,” and tells Karthik the same about Riya, so they never collaborate.

• Constant comparisons with a sibling, colleague or ex
• Messages passed through others instead of said to you
• You feel in competition with someone you've never had an issue with
• Gossip that pits people against each other

• Go direct: “If you have a concern about my work, please tell me directly.”
• Talk to the 'third person' honestly; often you'll discover the game
• Don't compete for approval; focus on your own standards
• Refuse to carry messages: “I think you should tell her that yourself.”

lessons.action: If someone compares you to another person today, notice how it makes you feel and whether it's meant to motivate or to control.

quiz.q: Triangulation is…
options: Using a third person to create jealousy, competition or pressure
Asking a mediator for help fairly
quiz.why: The third person becomes a tool for control.

quiz.q: Your manager tells you and a teammate privately that the other is 'much better', so you never trust each other. Which is this?
quiz.why: He's pitting you against a third person.

quiz.q: A healthy response?
options: Work harder to beat the other person
Ask for direct communication and talk openly with the other person
quiz.why: Going direct breaks the triangle.

lessons.title: Love bombing
lessons.summary: Too much, too fast, too perfect: when affection is used as a hook.

term.meaning: Overwhelming someone with intense attention, flattery, gifts and promises early on, to create quick attachment and dependence.

sections.b: Imagine meeting someone who, within two weeks, calls you their soulmate, texts all day, sends gifts and plans your future together. It feels like a movie. The problem: real trust takes time. In unhealthy patterns, the intense phase is followed by control, criticism or withdrawal once you're hooked. Not every enthusiastic new partner is manipulative; the warning sign is speed plus pressure plus a later switch.

On a dating app, Aakash meets Nisha. By week two he's sent flowers to her office, says “I've never felt this way about anyone,” and wants to meet her parents. When Nisha says she wants to slow down, he sulks: “I thought you were different.” A new company recruiter showers praise, then pushes for an immediate joining decision.

• Intensity that feels much faster than the relationship's age
• Huge compliments before they really know you
• Pressure to commit quickly (move in, meet family, decide now)
• Hurt or anger when you set a small boundary

• Slow it down on purpose and watch how they react
• Keep your usual routines and friends; don't drop everything
• Script: “I like you, and I want to take this at a slower pace.”
• Ask trusted friends what they see; if you feel controlled or unsafe, reach out to a counsellor or Tele-MANAS (14416)

lessons.action: Think of a time something felt 'too good, too fast'. What did slowing down reveal?

quiz.q: Love bombing is…
options: Overwhelming affection early on to create quick attachment
quiz.why: It's intensity used to hook someone.

quiz.q: Your new match texts 100 times a day, says 'you're my soulmate' in week one, and gets angry when you need a day off. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Intensity plus anger at a boundary is a warning sign.

quiz.q: A healthy test?
options: Slow things down and see how they respond to the boundary
Make a big commitment to prove love
Cut off your friends to focus on them
quiz.why: Respect for a slower pace is a good sign; anger is not.

lessons.title: The double bind
lessons.summary: Heads they win, tails you lose: when every choice is the wrong one.

term.meaning: A situation where someone gives you conflicting demands so that any response you choose will be criticised.

sections.b: Picture a parent saying 'Be independent!' and then getting upset whenever you make your own decision. Whatever you do, you're wrong. Because you can't win, you start feeling anxious and stuck. Sometimes it's unintentional, people are confusing, but when it's repeated it becomes a way to keep you off balance.

Siya's manager says, “Take initiative, don't wait for me,” but when she takes a decision, he snaps, “Why didn't you check with me first?” At home, Siya's mother says, “Do whatever you want with your career,” then cries for days when Siya chooses a job in another city.

• Two messages that cancel each other out
• You feel blamed no matter what you choose
• Questions like “Do you love me or your friends?” with no fair answer
• Anxiety before every small decision

• Name it calmly: “I'm getting two different messages. Which matters more here?”
• Ask for clear, written expectations at work
• You can refuse the false choice: “I can care about both.”
• Accept that you can't please a no-win demand; aim for what's reasonable

lessons.action: When you next feel 'damned if I do, damned if I don't', write down the two messages and ask for clarity.

quiz.q: A double bind is…
options: Conflicting demands where any choice gets criticised
quiz.why: Every option is set up to fail.

quiz.q: Your boss says 'Don't bother me with small things' and later 'Why didn't you tell me about this small issue?' Which is this?
quiz.why: Conflicting demands make you wrong either way.

quiz.q: Best response?
options: Do the opposite of what's asked
Name the conflict and ask which priority matters more
quiz.why: Asking for clarity breaks the bind.

lessons.title: DARVO
lessons.summary: Deny it, attack you, then act like the victim. Classic flip.

term.meaning: Short for Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender: a reaction where someone confronted about their behaviour denies it, attacks the person raising it, and claims they are the real victim.

sections.b: You calmly say, 'You shouted at me in front of the team.' They reply: 'I did not (Deny). You're so dramatic, always creating problems (Attack). Honestly, I'm the one being bullied here (Reverse Victim and Offender).' Suddenly you're apologising for bringing it up. The term was coined by psychologist Jennifer Freyd. People get defensive sometimes; DARVO is when it's a repeated pattern that shuts down accountability.

Pallavi tells her cousin that his jokes about her weight hurt her. He says, “I never said anything like that. You're always so negative. Now everyone will think I'm the bad guy because of you.” Soon relatives are asking Pallavi to 'adjust' and apologise.

• Your complaint turns into a discussion about your flaws
• You end up apologising after raising a real issue
• They play hurt and get others to sympathise with them
• The original behaviour is never actually addressed

• Stay on the original point: “I'm talking about what happened on Monday.”
• Don't defend yourself against every attack; repeat your concern calmly
• Keep records, especially at work, and use HR or formal channels where needed
• Get support from people who saw what happened, or a counsellor

lessons.action: If a conversation suddenly flips onto you, quietly ask yourself: what was the original issue?

quiz.q: What does DARVO stand for?
options: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender
quiz.why: It describes a denial-plus-attack-plus-victim flip.

quiz.q: You report a colleague's rude emails. He denies it, says you're 'out to get him', and tells the team he's being targeted. Which is this?
quiz.why: Deny, attack, then reverse victim and offender.

quiz.q: Best response to DARVO?
options: Calmly return to the original issue and keep records
quiz.why: Staying on point and documenting prevents the flip.

lessons.title: Guilt-tripping
lessons.summary: 'After all I've done for you…' is often the start of a guilt trip.

term.meaning: Using guilt to pressure someone into doing what you want, instead of asking directly.

sections.b: Everyone feels guilt, and healthy guilt helps us fix real mistakes. Guilt-tripping is different: guilt is used as a lever. 'Fine, go enjoy, I'll just sit alone.' It makes saying no feel like a crime. Many of us grew up with this, often from people who love us and learned it themselves, so it can be done without bad intent.

Rohan wants to spend Diwali with his wife's family this year. His mother says, “Do what you want. We're old, who knows how many Diwalis we have left.” At work, a manager sighs, “I guess I'll just stay till midnight again, since nobody else cares about this project,” to get people to volunteer.

• Sighs, sad comments or reminders of past favours when you say no
• “After all I've done…” or “I guess I don't matter”
• You say yes, then feel resentful
• Requests are never made directly

• Separate the feeling from the decision: “I can feel guilty and still say no.”
• Respond with warmth plus a boundary: “I love you, and this year we're going to her parents'. Let's plan a special day with you too.”
• Ask for direct requests: “Is there something you'd like me to do?”
• Check: is this guilt about a real wrong, or about disappointing someone?

lessons.action: Notice one 'yes' this week that you gave out of guilt, and how it felt afterwards.

quiz.q: Guilt-tripping is…
options: Using guilt as pressure instead of asking directly
quiz.why: Guilt is used as a lever for control.

quiz.q: When you decline a weekend plan, your friend says, 'It's fine, I'm used to being nobody's priority.' Which is this?
quiz.why: It uses guilt to change your decision.

quiz.q: A good response combines…
quiz.why: You can be kind and still hold your decision.

lessons.title: Stonewalling & the silent treatment
lessons.summary: Taking a break to cool down is healthy. Using silence as a punishment is not.

term.meaning: Withdrawing communication, refusing to respond or ignoring someone, often as a way to punish or control them.

sections.b: Sometimes people go quiet because they're overwhelmed and need space; relationship researcher John Gottman calls shutting down in conflict 'stonewalling', and it's often a sign of flooding, not evil. The silent treatment becomes manipulative when silence is used to punish: you're ignored for days until you apologise, often without knowing what you did. The difference: a healthy break says “I need time, let's talk tonight”; a punishment just goes cold.

After Meera says she's going on a girls' trip, her husband stops talking to her for four days, answers in single words and leaves the room when she enters. Eventually she cancels the trip and apologises. At work, a team lead ignores one member's messages for a week after she disagrees with him in a meeting.

• Days of silence after you set a boundary or disagree
• You don't know what you did, but you're expected to fix it
• Silence ends only when you apologise or give in
• Cold, ignoring behaviour in front of others

• Script: “I can see you're upset. I'm ready to talk when you are.” Then live your life
• Don't beg or over-apologise for things you didn't do
• If you are the one shutting down, say “I need 30 minutes, then let's talk”
• At work, keep communication in writing and loop in your manager or HR if it blocks your work; if it's part of a wider pattern of control, talk to a counsellor

lessons.action: If you ever go quiet in an argument, practise saying 'I need a break, let's talk at 8' instead.

quiz.q: What separates a healthy break from the silent treatment?
options: A healthy break is communicated and time-bound; silent treatment is used as punishment
The silent treatment is always unintentional
quiz.why: Communication and intent make the difference.

quiz.q: Your partner refuses to speak to you for three days after you say no to a plan, until you apologise. Which is this?
quiz.why: Silence is being used to punish and pressure.

quiz.q: Good script?
options: 'I can see you're upset. I'm ready to talk when you are.'
'Fine, I'll never speak to you either.'
quiz.why: It stays calm and leaves the door open without giving in.

lessons.title: Moving the goalposts
lessons.summary: You hit the target. Suddenly the target moved.

term.meaning: Changing the standard or requirement after someone has met it, so they can never quite succeed.

sections.b: Imagine scoring a goal in football and the referee says, 'Ah, but now it only counts if you score from the halfway line.' That's moving the goalposts. In real life it keeps you chasing approval that never comes. Sometimes goals change for genuine reasons (business needs shift); the pattern to watch is when it always happens right after you succeed.

Varun is told he'll get a promotion if he hits ₹50 lakh in sales. He hits ₹55 lakh, and now he's told he also needs 'more leadership visibility'. Next cycle it's 'a certification'. In family life, a parent says, “Get a good job and we'll stop worrying,” then “Now get married,” then “Now buy a flat.”

• New conditions appear right after you meet the old ones
• Promises like “once you do X, then…” never arrive
• The criteria were never written down
• You feel exhausted and never 'enough'

• Get goals and criteria in writing, with dates
• When it shifts, name it: “We agreed on X, and I've achieved it. What's changed?”
• Decide your own definition of 'enough'
• If it keeps happening at work, consider whether this environment will ever reward you

lessons.action: Write down one goal you're working towards and the exact, agreed criteria for 'done'.

quiz.q: Moving the goalposts means…
options: Changing the requirement after someone meets it
quiz.why: The target moves so success never arrives.

quiz.q: Your manager promised a raise after a certification; you got it, and now he says you need two more years. Which is this?
quiz.why: The condition changed after you met it.

quiz.q: Best protection?
options: Get criteria in writing and refer back to them
quiz.why: Written criteria make shifting visible.

lessons.title: Breadcrumbing
lessons.summary: Just enough attention to keep you hoping, never enough to go anywhere.

term.meaning: Giving someone small, occasional bits of attention (likes, 'hey' texts, vague plans) to keep them interested without any real commitment.

sections.b: Like dropping breadcrumbs for a pigeon: never a full meal, just enough to keep it following. A breadcrumber replies late at night, likes your stories, says “we should meet sometime”, but never actually shows up. It's often more about their convenience or ego than evil planning, but the effect on you is the same: stuck hoping.

Ishita matched with Kabir three months ago. Every week or two he sends “Hey stranger 😊” or likes her photo, but every plan to meet gets 'busy this week, let's do next'. In work, a recruiter keeps saying “There's definitely a role for you, let's connect soon” for six months without any interview.

• Communication is random and on their schedule only
• Lots of vague 'soon' and 'sometime', no actual plans
• You overanalyse small messages
• You feel more anxious than happy when you think about them

• Ask for clarity: “I'd love to meet. Are you free Saturday?” Their response tells you everything
• Judge by actions, not texts
• Set a time limit for yourself to see real effort
• It's okay to step away: “I'm looking for something more consistent. Take care.”

lessons.action: Think of one connection where you're running on crumbs, and decide what 'enough' looks like.

quiz.q: Breadcrumbing is…
options: Small, occasional attention without real commitment
quiz.why: Crumbs keep you hoping without moving forward.

quiz.q: Someone likes all your stories and says 'let's meet soon', but cancels every plan for months. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Minimal attention, no follow-through.

quiz.q: Best test?
options: Propose a specific plan and judge the response by actions
Wait longer for them to decide
quiz.why: Specific plans reveal real intent.

lessons.title: Future faking
lessons.summary: Big promises about tomorrow, used to get what they want today.

term.meaning: Making exciting promises about the future (trips, marriage, promotions) with no real plan to keep them, to keep you attached or compliant now.

sections.b: 'Next year we'll go to Europe.' 'Once the funding comes, you'll be a partner.' Future plans are normal and lovely. Future faking is when the promises keep coming but nothing concrete ever happens, and the promises appear exactly when you're about to leave or push back. It works because hope is powerful.

Each time Neha talks about leaving, her boyfriend says, “By December we'll talk to our parents and get engaged.” December comes and goes. At a startup, the founder tells Aman, “Take a lower salary now, you'll get big ESOPs next round,” but there's nothing in writing.

• Promises get bigger exactly when you're unhappy
• Plans never turn into concrete steps (dates, bookings, documents)
• Questions about details are met with “Why don't you trust me?”
• A long history of promises not kept

• Ask for one small concrete step now (book the date, sign the letter)
• Get work promises like ESOPs or raises in writing
• Judge by their track record, not their words
• Script: “I'd love that. What's the first step and when?”

lessons.action: List one promise someone made you, and whether any concrete step has happened.

quiz.q: Future faking is…
options: Big future promises with no real plan, used to control the present
quiz.why: The promise is the tool, not the intention.

quiz.q: Your boss keeps promising 'next quarter you'll lead the team' whenever you mention leaving, but nothing changes. Which is this?
quiz.why: Promises appear to keep you, without action.

quiz.q: Best counter-move?
options: Ask for a concrete first step with a date, in writing
quiz.why: Concrete steps separate real plans from fake ones.

lessons.title: Hoovering
lessons.summary: When they suddenly come back just as you've moved on.

term.meaning: Attempts by someone you've distanced yourself from to pull you back into the relationship, often with apologies, nostalgia or sudden crises.

sections.b: Named after the Hoover vacuum cleaner: they try to suck you back in. After you leave or set a firm boundary, you suddenly get a sweet text on your birthday, a dramatic “I've changed”, or a crisis that only you can solve. Sometimes people genuinely change. But if the pattern is: return, short honeymoon, same behaviour, then it's hoovering.

Two months after Ritika ends a toxic relationship, her ex sends, “Saw our song on the radio. I miss you. I've been in therapy.” When she doesn't reply, he messages her best friend saying he's 'not okay'. A former boss who treated Dev badly calls with a 'special opportunity' after he joins a competitor.

• Contact appears right when you're doing well or moving on
• Nostalgic messages, sudden apologies or emergencies
• Promises of change with no real evidence
• Contact through friends or family when you go silent

• Remember why you left; keep a short note of the reasons
• Look for sustained change over time, not words
• You don't owe a reply. Options: mute, block, or one clear message: “I wish you well, but I'm not reopening this.”
• If there are threats or self-harm messages, contact local emergency services or a professional; Tele-MANAS (14416) can help you too

lessons.action: If you've distanced from someone, write down three reasons you did, so you can reread them if they reach out.

quiz.q: Hoovering is…
options: Trying to pull someone back after they've distanced themselves
Apologising once sincerely and respecting a no
quiz.why: Named after the vacuum: sucking you back in.

quiz.q: Your ex, who cheated repeatedly, texts on your birthday saying 'I've changed, I need you' right after you start dating someone. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Timed contact to pull you back.

quiz.q: What's a healthy sign of real change?
options: Consistent changed behaviour over a long time
quiz.why: Actions over time matter more than words.

lessons.title: Flying monkeys
lessons.summary: When someone sends other people to do their pressuring for them.

term.meaning: People who, knowingly or not, carry messages, guilt or pressure on behalf of someone else who's trying to control you.

sections.b: The term comes from The Wizard of Oz, where the witch sends flying monkeys to do her work. In real life, a person you've set a boundary with might recruit relatives, friends or colleagues to 'talk sense into you'. Most flying monkeys aren't villains; they've usually only heard one side and genuinely think they're helping.

After Karan stops lending money to his uncle, three relatives call him in one week: “He's family, how can you be so cold?” At work, after Pooja raises a complaint about her team lead, two colleagues start telling her, “He's actually really stressed, maybe you should drop it.”

• Many people suddenly bring up the same issue
• They repeat phrases that clearly came from one source
• You're asked to 'just apologise' without being asked your side
• You feel ganged up on after setting a boundary

• Don't get into a long debate with every messenger
• Script: “I appreciate you caring. This is between me and him, and I've made my decision.”
• Share your side only with people you trust, if at all
• Lean on your support system; you don't need everyone to agree with you

lessons.action: If someone brings you a message 'on behalf of' someone else, notice it and decide if you want to engage.

quiz.q: 'Flying monkeys' are…
options: People pressuring you on someone else's behalf
Neutral mediators who hear both sides
quiz.why: They carry someone else's pressure.

quiz.q: After you set a boundary with your aunt, four relatives message you saying you're 'heartless' using her exact words. Which is this?
quiz.why: Others are delivering her pressure.

quiz.q: A good response?
options: Argue with each person in detail
Thank them for caring and keep your boundary without debating
quiz.why: Short, calm, firm replies conserve your energy.

lessons.title: Projection
lessons.summary: Sometimes what people accuse you of says more about them.

term.meaning: Unconsciously putting your own unwanted feelings, traits or behaviours onto someone else.

sections.b: It's like someone who hates their own jealousy but keeps saying, 'Why are you always so jealous?' Projection is a normal mental defence everyone uses a bit, because it's easier to see a flaw in others than in ourselves. It becomes a problem when someone repeatedly accuses you of exactly the things they're doing. Careful: not every accusation is projection; sometimes feedback is fair.

Ajay keeps checking his partner's phone and accusing her of cheating, while he's the one hiding chats. At work, a colleague who often takes credit for others' work loudly warns everyone that Sana is 'a credit-stealer'.

• Accusations that oddly match the accuser's own behaviour
• Strong emotional reactions to small things you did
• You're blamed for feelings they won't own
• A pattern of the same accusation without evidence

• Ask yourself honestly: “Is there truth in this feedback?” If yes, own it
• If not, stay calm: “I don't see it that way. Can you give me an example?”
• Don't absorb the label; check with people who know you
• Notice your own projection too: what irritates you most in others?

lessons.action: Think of one trait that really annoys you in others, and gently check if it lives in you too.

quiz.q: Projection is…
options: Placing your own unwanted feelings or behaviour onto others
quiz.why: It's a defence that moves our own stuff onto others.

quiz.q: A coworker who often misses deadlines keeps accusing you of being 'unreliable' with no examples. Which is this possibly?
quiz.why: The accusation matches his own behaviour.

quiz.q: Best first step when accused?
options: Honestly check if there's truth in it, then respond calmly
quiz.why: Not every accusation is projection; self-check first.

lessons.title: Intermittent reinforcement & trauma bonding
lessons.summary: Why the hot-and-cold relationships are the hardest ones to leave.

term.meaning: Unpredictable rewards (affection, praise) mixed with bad treatment, which creates a strong, hard-to-break attachment.

sections.b: Slot machines are addictive because you never know when you'll win. Relationships can work the same: if someone is sometimes loving and sometimes cruel, your brain stays hooked waiting for the next 'good' moment. Over time this can create a 'trauma bond', a strong attachment to someone who also hurts you. It's not a weakness; it's how brains respond to unpredictable rewards.

Simran's boyfriend ignores her for days, criticises her clothes, then suddenly surprises her with a lovely dinner and says she's his whole world. She holds on to the dinner memory for weeks. At a job, a boss who yells most days but occasionally gives glowing praise keeps an employee desperate for that rare approval.

• You live for the rare good moments
• The bad times are frequent, but you remember the good ones more
• You feel anxious and on edge, trying to keep them happy
• You defend them to friends who are worried

• Write down how most days actually feel, not just the highlights
• Talk to trusted friends or a counsellor who can give an outside view
• Reduce contact gradually if you can, to let the hook weaken
• If there's any abuse or safety risk, reach out to a professional, Tele-MANAS (14416), or emergency services (112)

lessons.action: If a relationship feels like a rollercoaster, keep a simple daily note for a week: good day or bad day?

quiz.q: Why is intermittent reinforcement so 'sticky'?
options: Because the person is always kind
Unpredictable rewards keep the brain hooked, like a slot machine
quiz.why: Not knowing when the next reward comes makes it powerful.

quiz.q: Your friend's partner is cold for weeks then suddenly very loving, and she says 'he's amazing when he's good'. What is this most like?
quiz.why: Hot-and-cold treatment creates a strong hook.

quiz.q: A helpful step?
options: Wait for the next good moment
Track how most days actually feel and talk to trusted people
quiz.why: An honest record and outside support weaken the bond.

lessons.title: Weaponised incompetence
lessons.summary: 'I'm just bad at this' can be a clever way to make you do it forever.

term.meaning: Pretending to be bad at a task, or doing it badly on purpose, so someone else ends up doing it.

sections.b: Some people genuinely struggle with tasks, that's fine. Weaponised incompetence is when someone can learn but chooses not to, because looking clueless gets them out of it. 'You're so much better at it!' sounds like a compliment, but it's a trap. It's common with chores, admin work and 'boring' tasks at the office.

Rakesh 'can't' figure out how to use the washing machine, so his wife does all the laundry, though he manages a team of 20 and handles complex software daily. At work, Sunil formats reports so badly that the manager says, “Just let Priya do the formatting from now on.”

• “You do it better” used to dodge tasks
• Simple tasks are done badly again and again, without improving
• The person is capable in other, more complex areas
• The same people always end up with the boring work

• Teach once, clearly, then step back and let them do it, even if imperfectly
• Don't 'rescue' or redo small things
• Script: “I showed you last time. I trust you to handle it.”
• At work, assign ownership clearly and in writing

lessons.action: Look at your week: is there a task you always do because someone else 'can't'?

quiz.q: Weaponised incompetence is…
options: Acting unable to do a task so someone else does it
Genuinely struggling with a hard skill
quiz.why: It's strategic helplessness.

quiz.q: Your flatmate, a software engineer, says he 'just can't' figure out the electricity bill app, so you always pay it. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: He's capable but uses 'incompetence' to avoid the task.

quiz.q: Good response?
options: Teach once, then let them own it
quiz.why: Ownership breaks the pattern.

lessons.title: Negging & backhanded compliments
lessons.summary: 'You're pretty smart for someone from a small town.' That's not a compliment.

term.meaning: Mixing a compliment with a small insult, to lower someone's confidence and make them seek approval.

sections.b: A backhanded compliment sounds nice but has a sting inside: 'You look great today, did you finally go to the gym?' 'Negging' is the deliberate version, often used in dating to make someone feel slightly less confident so they try harder to impress. Some people just have clumsy humour; the pattern to watch is regular digs that leave you feeling small.

On a date, Vikas tells Sneha, “You're actually funny, I didn't expect that from someone who works in HR.” A relative at a wedding says to Priya, “Wow, you've become so fair, the Mumbai weather suits you.” A senior says, “Good presentation, I'm surprised you pulled it off.”

• Compliments that leave you feeling worse
• Comparisons that put you or your group down
• 'Just joking' after the sting
• You find yourself trying harder to win their approval

• Name the sting gently: “That sounded like a compliment and an insult. Which did you mean?”
• Or respond only to the positive part: “Thanks!” and move on
• Don't chase approval from people who regularly put you down
• Spend more time with people whose compliments are clean

lessons.action: Notice any 'compliment' this week that left a bitter aftertaste.

quiz.q: Negging is…
options: A compliment mixed with a subtle insult to lower confidence
quiz.why: The insult is hidden inside praise.

quiz.q: Your colleague says, 'Nice work! I didn't think you could handle such a big client.' Which is this?
quiz.why: Praise with a built-in dig.

quiz.q: A calm response option?
options: 'That sounded like a compliment and an insult. Which did you mean?'
quiz.why: Naming it gently puts the sting back on the speaker.

lessons.title: Word salad & circular arguments
lessons.summary: When a conversation goes round and round and you leave more confused than you started.

term.meaning: A confusing flood of words, topic jumps and contradictions in an argument that leaves you disoriented, so the real issue is never resolved.

sections.b: You raise one simple issue. Suddenly you're discussing something from 2019, your tone, their feelings, a philosophy of life, and back to your tone. Two hours later you're exhausted and nothing is solved. In clinical psychology 'word salad' means something different (disorganised speech in some conditions); here we mean the everyday pattern of muddy, circular arguing that blocks accountability.

Aisha asks her partner why he didn't come to her office party as promised. He replies: “You always do this. Remember when you forgot my mother's birthday? And honestly, parties are so fake, and you know I've had a tough week, and why are you even like this when I support you so much?” The party question is never answered.

• Topic keeps switching every time you get close to the point
• Old issues are dragged in to avoid the current one
• Contradictions that make you doubt your own logic
• You walk away tired and confused, with nothing resolved

• Keep it to one issue: “I want to talk about just this one thing.”
• Gently bring it back: “Let's park that. About the party…”
• End the loop: “We're going in circles. Let's pause and come back tomorrow.”
• Write your main point before the talk so you don't lose it

lessons.action: Before your next hard conversation, write your one main point on a sticky note.

quiz.q: In everyday manipulation talk, 'word salad' means…
options: A medical diagnosis anyone can give
Confusing, circular arguing that avoids the real issue
quiz.why: It's muddy talk that blocks resolution.

quiz.q: You ask your colleague why he missed a client call and he goes into a long talk about company culture, your attitude and last year's appraisal. Which is this most like?
quiz.why: Topic-jumping avoids the actual question.

quiz.q: Best way to handle it?
options: Bring up your own old issues
Stick to one issue and pause if it keeps circling
quiz.why: Focus and pausing break the loop.

lessons.title: Foot-in-the-door & door-in-the-face
lessons.summary: Two classic tricks: start tiny and grow, or start huge and 'compromise'.

term.meaning: Persuasion techniques: asking for a small yes first to get a bigger yes later, or asking for something huge first so a smaller request seems reasonable.

sections.b: Foot-in-the-door: once you've said yes to something small, saying no to the next step feels inconsistent, so you keep agreeing. Door-in-the-face: they ask for something crazy, you say no, then their 'smaller' request feels like a fair compromise and you feel you should meet them halfway. Both have research behind them, though results vary. Salespeople, charities and colleagues use them, often without realising.

Foot-in-the-door: a colleague asks Nidhi to “just review one slide”, then “just fix the formatting”, then “could you present it since you know it so well?” Door-in-the-face: a cousin asks Arjun to lend ₹2 lakh. He refuses. “Okay, at least ₹30,000?” Arjun agrees, though he'd never have lent that if asked first.

• A series of small asks that keep growing
• Feeling you 'have to' continue because you said yes before
• A huge first request followed quickly by a 'smaller' one
• Feeling guilty for refusing, so you agree to the second ask

• Judge each request on its own: “Would I say yes if this were the first ask?”
• It's fine to stop halfway: “I helped with the slide, but I can't present.”
• After a big no, pause before answering the smaller request
• Buy time: “Let me check and get back to you.”

lessons.action: Next time you get a 'small favour' request, ask what the next request might be.

quiz.q: Foot-in-the-door means…
options: Starting with a small request to make a bigger one more likely
quiz.why: A small yes creates pressure for a bigger yes.

quiz.q: A salesman offers a ₹90,000 phone plan; you refuse; he then offers a ₹25,000 plan and you take it, feeling you 'compromised'. Which technique is this?
quiz.why: The big first ask made the second seem reasonable.

quiz.q: Best defence for both?
options: Judge each request as if it were the first
Always say yes to stay polite
Ask for a bigger favour back
quiz.why: Evaluating each request fresh breaks both tricks.

lessons.title: Emotional blackmail (FOG)
lessons.summary: Fear, Obligation and Guilt: the fog that makes 'no' feel impossible.

term.meaning: Using fear, obligation or guilt (FOG) to pressure someone into doing what you want, often with a hidden or open threat.

sections.b: Therapist Susan Forward described emotional blackmail using the word FOG: Fear (“If you do this, something bad will happen”), Obligation (“You owe me”), and Guilt (“You'll be responsible if I'm hurt”).
