If it helps at all, it's because writing something many times keeps it on your mind, which is just a fancy reminder. The risk is spending your energy on the ritual instead of the work.

Vikram writes 'I will clear CAT with 99 percentile' 18 times a day for 33 days. It takes him about 20 minutes daily. His friend uses those same 20 minutes to solve one quant set. On exam day, only one of those habits shows up in the score.

• Viral posts saying Tesla 'unlocked the universe' with 3, 6, 9
• Strict rules like 'it fails if you miss a day'
• Feeling guilty or anxious about doing the ritual wrong
• Using the ritual as proof you're 'working on' the goal

• If you like it, keep it short and pair it with an action ('...and today I'll do X')
• Notice if the ritual is replacing real effort
• Ignore the 'it won't work if you break the streak' rule; there's no evidence for it
• A daily reminder or alarm does the same job in 10 seconds

lessons.action: Replace one ritual or wish with a 10-minute action on the same goal today.

quiz.q: Is there evidence Nikola Tesla created the 369 manifesting method?
quiz.why: The Tesla link spread online without any reliable source.

quiz.q: If the 369 method helps someone, the most likely reason is...
options: Repetition keeps the goal on their mind
quiz.why: It works like a reminder, nothing more mysterious.

quiz.q: What's the main risk of rituals like this?
quiz.why: Time spent on the ritual can feel like progress without being progress.

lessons.title: Visualisation & mental rehearsal
lessons.summary: Athletes picture the game before playing. The trick is picturing the right thing.

term.meaning: Practising a task in your mind, step by step, to prepare for doing it for real.

sections.b: Many athletes, from cricketers to Olympic swimmers, practise in their heads: the run-up, the grip, the release. Research shows mental practice can improve performance, though less than real practice; it works best combined with it. The key is what you picture. In a classic 1998 study, students who imagined the process (sitting at the desk, reading notes) studied more and scored better than students who only imagined the outcome (seeing a great grade). Picture the steps, not just the trophy.

Arjun has a salary negotiation on Friday. Outcome visualisation: he pictures the HR person saying 'Yes, 40% hike!' and feels great. Process visualisation: he mentally walks through opening the call, stating his number, staying quiet after, and handling 'that's above our budget'. On Friday he's calm because his brain has 'been there' before.

• Outcome visualisation: picturing only the win, the applause, the result
• Process visualisation: picturing the actions, the hard moments, your response
• Feeling hyped after visualising but no better prepared is a sign you only pictured the outcome
• Athletes call it 'rehearsal' because it's practice, not wishing

• Picture the task step by step in real time, with details (room, voice, your words)
• Include a tough moment and see yourself handling it
• Combine it with real practice, like a mock call with a friend
• Keep it short: 2 to 5 minutes before the event is enough

lessons.action: Before your next meeting or call, close your eyes for 2 minutes and rehearse the opening, one tricky question, and your answer.

quiz.q: In the 1998 study, which students did better?
options: Those who imagined the steps of studying
Those who imagined getting a great grade
quiz.why: Process simulation led to more studying and better scores.

quiz.q: Mental rehearsal works best when...
options: It focuses only on the reward
quiz.why: Mental practice helps, but real practice still matters more.

quiz.q: Which is process visualisation?
options: Rehearsing how you'll answer a tough interview question
Seeing your name on the leaderboard
quiz.why: It focuses on the actions and moments you must handle.

lessons.title: WOOP / mental contrasting
lessons.summary: Dream big, then picture what's in the way. This combo actually has research behind it.

term.meaning: A goal method: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan, based on mental contrasting and if-then planning.

sections.b: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen found that just dreaming about success can lower your energy, but pairing the dream with the main obstacle wakes you up. She turned this into WOOP: Wish (what you want), Outcome (the best result, felt vividly), Obstacle (the thing inside you most likely to stop you), Plan ('If obstacle happens, then I'll do X'). That last part is called an implementation intention, and studies across many goals show if-then plans help people follow through. It's simple, free and takes 5 minutes.

Wish: Neha wants to go to the gym 3 times a week. Outcome: more energy, less back pain from sitting all day. Obstacle: she gets home at 8, feels tired and opens Netflix. Plan: 'If I feel too tired after work, then I'll put on my gym shoes and do just 15 minutes.' Most days, once the shoes are on, she does the full workout.

• You've dreamed about a goal for ages but never named what actually stops you
• Your obstacle is something outside you that you can't control (pick an inner one instead)
• Your plan is vague like 'try harder' instead of 'if X, then Y'
• You skip the outcome step and feel no pull toward the goal

• Do all four steps in order, in your head or on paper, in about 5 minutes
• Pick the obstacle inside you: a habit, emotion or excuse
• Write the plan as 'If [obstacle], then I will [specific action]'
• Use WOOP for one goal at a time, and redo it when things change

lessons.action: Run one WOOP right now on something you want this week. Say the If-then plan out loud once.

quiz.q: What does the second O in WOOP stand for?
quiz.why: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan.

quiz.q: Which is a good WOOP plan?
options: If I want to scroll at 11 pm, then I'll put my phone in the kitchen
quiz.why: A specific if-then plan links a trigger to an action.

quiz.q: Why add obstacles instead of only dreaming?
options: Contrasting dream and obstacle boosts energy and follow-through
quiz.why: Mental contrasting turns a pleasant fantasy into readiness to act.

lessons.title: Self-fulfilling prophecy
lessons.summary: Expect something strongly enough and you might accidentally make it happen.

term.meaning: When a belief about what will happen changes your behaviour in a way that makes it come true.

sections.b: If you believe a new teammate is lazy, you might give them boring work and less help, and then they really do seem unmotivated. Your belief created the result. This also works in a good way: a famous 1968 study (the 'Pygmalion effect') suggested teachers' high expectations helped students do better, though later research found the real effect is smaller than first claimed. The point is that expectations, yours and other people's, quietly change actions. This is the scientific cousin of manifesting: no magic, just behaviour.

Siddharth is sure the quarterly review will go badly. He walks in defensive, gives short answers and doesn't share his wins. His manager reads him as disengaged, and the review does go badly. His expectation shaped his behaviour, which shaped the outcome.

• 'I knew this would happen' after you acted in a way that made it more likely
• Treating someone as a problem and then seeing them act like one
• Avoiding preparation because 'it won't work anyway'
• Also good versions: a manager's trust making a junior step up

• When you predict failure, ask: how is this belief changing what I'm doing?
• Act 'as if' it could go okay: prepare, show up, speak up
• Give new people a fair start; your expectations affect them
• Remember it's not guaranteed; it nudges odds, it doesn't decide fate

lessons.action: Think of one situation you're expecting to go badly, and write one action you'd take if you expected it to go well. Do that action.

quiz.q: How does a self-fulfilling prophecy work?
options: Beliefs change behaviour, which changes outcomes
It only works with predictions about weather
quiz.why: The belief works through actions, not magic.

quiz.q: What did later research say about the Pygmalion effect?
options: It was proven fake in every way
It's real but smaller than first claimed
quiz.why: Teacher expectation effects exist but are usually modest.

quiz.q: Siddharth's review went badly mainly because...
options: His negative expectation made him act defensive
quiz.why: His behaviour, shaped by his belief, created the result.

lessons.title: Placebo & nocebo effects
lessons.summary: Sugar pills can make you feel better, and warnings can make you feel worse.

term.meaning: Placebo is feeling better because you expect a treatment to work; nocebo is feeling worse because you expect harm.

sections.b: A placebo is a fake treatment, like a sugar pill, that can still make people report less pain or better mood because they expect it to help. Its effects are real but limited: mostly on symptoms you feel, like pain, nausea or tiredness, not on things like tumours or infections. Nocebo is the dark twin: reading a long list of side effects can make people actually feel some of them. Your expectations really do change how your body feels, which is why mindset matters, but they don't replace real medicine.

After reading online that a new medicine 'causes headaches', Ravi gets a headache on day one, even though his doctor later says it's rare. Meanwhile his mom swears her 'special' balm cures her knee pain; it may be partly placebo, which is fine for mild pain, but she shouldn't skip the physiotherapy her doctor recommended.

• Feeling relief before a medicine could even have started working
• Feeling side effects right after reading about them
• Expensive 'wellness' products that work mostly because they feel premium
• Claims that belief alone can cure serious illness (it can't)

• Use expectation in your favour: a calm, positive frame can make pain and stress feel lighter
• Don't doom-read side effect lists; ask your doctor what's common and what's rare
• Never drop real treatment for a 'mind over matter' cure
• Interesting fact: even 'open-label' placebos (people know it's a placebo) have helped in some studies, like for IBS

lessons.action: Next time you take something for a headache, notice whether you feel relief before it could chemically act. That's expectation at work.

quiz.q: Placebo effects mostly work on...
options: Symptoms you feel, like pain or nausea
quiz.why: Placebos change perceived symptoms, not underlying disease.

quiz.q: What is a nocebo effect?
options: Feeling better from a fake pill
Feeling worse because you expect harm
A medicine with no side effects
quiz.why: Negative expectations can create real symptoms.

quiz.q: What's the healthy takeaway?
options: Mindset helps, but doesn't replace real treatment
Always read every side effect online
quiz.why: Expectations matter, but within limits.

lessons.title: Growth mindset
lessons.summary: Believing you can improve helps. But the hype got way ahead of the science.

term.meaning: The belief that your abilities can grow with effort, good strategies and help.

sections.b: Psychologist Carol Dweck described two mindsets: fixed ('I'm just bad at Excel') and growth ('I'm bad at Excel yet'). The idea is solid and useful: if you think you can improve, you're more likely to practise and ask for help. But schools and companies hyped it as a miracle, and big reviews (like a 2018 meta-analysis) found the average effect of mindset training on grades is small, with larger benefits for some struggling students. Also, Dweck herself warns that 'growth mindset' isn't just praising effort; it's effort plus better strategies plus help.

Pooja thinks she's 'not a numbers person', so she avoids financial models at work. She shifts to 'I'm not good at this yet', takes a short course and asks a senior to review her model. Effort alone (staring at the sheet for hours) wouldn't have done it; effort plus a new strategy and feedback did.

• Fixed mindset lines: 'I'm just not a ___ person', 'Some people are naturally good'
• Fake growth mindset: praising effort even when the approach isn't working
• Companies using 'growth mindset' as a buzzword to push more hours
• Overselling: posts claiming mindset alone transforms your life

• Add 'yet' to self-judgements: 'I can't present well yet'
• When stuck, change the strategy, don't just try harder
• Ask for feedback; it's the fastest way to grow
• Keep expectations realistic: it's a helpful nudge, not a superpower

lessons.action: Catch one 'I'm not a ___ person' thought today and rewrite it with 'yet' plus one new strategy to try.

quiz.q: What did large reviews find about growth mindset training?
options: Small average effects, bigger for some groups
quiz.why: The effect is real but modest on average.

quiz.q: Which is a true growth mindset approach?
options: Effort plus new strategies plus help
quiz.why: Dweck stresses strategies and support, not just effort.

quiz.q: Which phrase shows a fixed mindset?
options: Can you show me how you did it?
I'm just not a coding person
quiz.why: It treats ability as permanent.

lessons.title: Locus of control
lessons.summary: Do you feel in charge of your life, or like life just happens to you?

term.meaning: How much you believe your outcomes are controlled by your own actions (internal) versus outside forces (external).

sections.b: Psychologist Julian Rotter described this in 1966. People with an internal locus think 'my effort decides my results'; people with an external locus think 'luck, the boss or fate decides'. Research links a more internal locus to things like better health habits and job satisfaction. But the truth is a mix: some things really are outside your control (layoffs, market crashes, your manager's mood). The healthiest version is: 'I control my actions and responses, not everything that happens.'

When layoffs hit his company, Aman thinks, 'It's all random, nothing I do matters,' and stops updating his skills. His friend Divya thinks, 'I can't stop layoffs, but I can update my resume, keep my network warm and save an emergency fund.' Same situation, different locus, very different next six months.

• External lines: 'What's the point?', 'It's all politics', 'Some people are just lucky'
• Extreme internal: blaming yourself for everything, even things you couldn't control
• Feeling helpless after a setback and stopping all effort
• Healthy middle: 'This part is on me, that part isn't'

• Split any problem into two lists: what I control, what I don't
• Spend your energy on the first list
• Don't beat yourself up over the second list
• Notice your 'it's all luck' thoughts and ask, 'What's one thing I can influence here?'

lessons.action: Take one current worry and write two columns: 'I control' and 'I don't'. Do one thing from the first column today.

quiz.q: Someone with an internal locus of control believes...
options: Their actions largely shape their results
quiz.why: Internal means outcomes are seen as driven by your own actions.

quiz.q: What's the healthiest version?
options: I control my actions and responses, not everything
quiz.why: Balanced control avoids both helplessness and self-blame.

quiz.q: During layoffs, what did Divya do differently?
options: Focused on what she could influence
quiz.why: She acted on her controllables: resume, network, savings.

lessons.title: Gratitude practice
lessons.summary: Writing down good things can lift your mood a little. It's not magic, but it's cheap.

term.meaning: Regularly noticing and noting things you're thankful for.

sections.b: A gratitude practice is simple: write down a few good things, or thank someone. Studies (like Emmons and McCullough, 2003) found people who did this felt a bit happier and more optimistic. Later reviews say the effects are real but modest, so think 'small daily vitamin', not 'cure'. Being specific helps ('my colleague covered my call so I could leave for my kid's PTM') more than generic lines ('I'm grateful for life'). And it's not about ignoring problems; you can be grateful and still want a raise.

Every night, Tanvi writes three specific things: the chai her flatmate made, a bug she finally fixed, a call with her nani. After a few weeks she notices she spots good moments during the day because she knows she'll write them down. Her stressful job is still stressful, but she feels a little lighter.

• Generic lists that feel like a chore ('family, health, job' every day)
• Using gratitude to guilt yourself ('others have it worse, so I shouldn't complain')
• Forced gratitude in toxic workplaces ('be grateful you have a job')
• Real gratitude feels specific and warm, not obligatory

• Write 3 specific good things, a few times a week (daily can get boring)
• Include why it happened or who made it happen
• Try a gratitude message: thank one person directly, which often lifts both of you
• Use it alongside fixing problems, not instead of it

lessons.action: Send one specific thank-you message to someone today, saying exactly what they did and how it helped.

quiz.q: What does research say about gratitude practice?
options: It gives real but modest boosts to mood
quiz.why: Effects are positive but small to moderate.

quiz.q: Which gratitude entry is more effective?
options: My teammate stayed late to help me debug before the demo
quiz.why: Specific details make gratitude feel real.

quiz.q: 'Be grateful you even have a job' when you raise a concern is...
options: Using gratitude to shut down valid complaints
quiz.why: Gratitude shouldn't be used to dismiss real problems.

lessons.title: Toxic positivity
lessons.summary: 'Just stay positive!' sounds kind but can make people feel worse.

term.meaning: Pushing for positive feelings in a way that dismisses or hides real negative emotions.

sections.b: Toxic positivity is when someone (or you) insists on 'good vibes only' even when things are genuinely hard. It sounds supportive, but it sends the message: your sadness or anger isn't allowed. Research on emotions suggests that trying to push down feelings often makes them stronger, while naming and accepting them helps them pass. Positivity is great; forced positivity is the problem.

After a layoff, Rohan posts in the team group that he's struggling. A colleague replies, 'Everything happens for a reason! Stay positive!' Rohan feels unheard and stops sharing. A better reply: 'That's really rough, man. Want to grab a call? Happy to refer you anywhere I can.'

• 'Just be positive', 'Others have it worse', 'Everything happens for a reason'
• Office culture that punishes people for raising problems
• Feeling guilty for being sad
• Social media where everyone is always 'blessed'

• Validate first: 'That sounds hard' before any advice
• Allow yourself to name feelings: 'I'm frustrated and that's okay'
• Offer help, not slogans
• Hope is fine; just don't use it to skip over someone's pain

lessons.action: Next time someone shares a problem, reply with one validating line before saying anything positive.

quiz.q: Toxic positivity is...
options: Dismissing real negative feelings with forced positivity
quiz.why: It's the dismissing, not the positivity, that's toxic.

quiz.q: Which reply is supportive?
options: That sounds really hard. How can I help?
quiz.why: Validation plus an offer of help.

quiz.q: What tends to happen when you push down negative emotions?
options: They often stay or get stronger
quiz.why: Suppression often backfires; acceptance helps feelings pass.

lessons.title: Lucky girl syndrome & luck
lessons.summary: Believing you're lucky won't bend the universe, but it might change what you notice.

term.meaning: A TikTok trend where people tell themselves they're lucky and expect good things to happen to them.

sections.b: Lucky girl syndrome went viral around 2022-23: say 'I'm so lucky, everything works out for me' and supposedly it does. The magic part has no evidence. But psychologist Richard Wiseman studied people who called themselves lucky and found they tended to be more relaxed, open and noticing. In one test, 'lucky' people were quicker to spot a big message in a newspaper saying 'stop counting, the answer is in here'. The old saying sums it up: luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.

Isha feels 'lucky' and says yes to a random networking dinner in Bengaluru. She chats with the person next to her, who turns out to be hiring. Was it luck? Partly. But she showed up, she was open, and her portfolio was ready to share. Someone who felt unlucky might have stayed home.

• Viral stories where only the lucky outcome is shown (survivorship bias)
• Ignoring privilege and effort behind 'I just got lucky' stories
• Using 'I'm lucky' to skip preparation
• Real 'lucky' habits: saying yes, talking to new people, noticing chances

• Increase your surface area: meet new people, share your work, try new things
• Prepare so you're ready when a chance shows up (updated resume, portfolio)
• Stay relaxed and curious; anxiety narrows what you notice
• After setbacks, ask 'what could I learn?' instead of 'why me?'

lessons.action: Do one 'surface area' thing today: comment thoughtfully on a post in your field or message someone new.

quiz.q: What did Richard Wiseman find about 'lucky' people?
quiz.why: Their openness helped them spot chances others missed.

quiz.q: 'Luck is what happens when preparation meets...'
quiz.why: Being ready plus a chance is what we call luck.

quiz.q: Why do viral 'lucky girl' stories mislead?
options: They only show the wins, not the misses
quiz.why: Survivorship bias hides everyone it didn't work for.

lessons.title: Delulu
lessons.summary: Short for delusional, and sometimes worn as a badge of honour.

term.meaning: Slang for delusional: believing something unrealistic, often about love, fame or success.

sections.b: Delulu started in K-pop fan circles, where fans joked about believing they'd marry their favourite idol. Now it's everywhere: 'I'm delulu thinking he'll text back.' 'Delulu is the solulu' (delusion is the solution) is a playful motto saying a bit of crazy confidence helps you chase big dreams. It's mostly used jokingly and self-aware. The catch: a little delulu can push you to try; a lot of delulu can make you ignore real signals.

Kavya applies to Google with two years of experience, saying, 'Delulu is the solulu.' That's fine; the worst they can say is no. But her friend who keeps waiting for a guy who hasn't replied in three weeks, saying 'he's just busy', is the risky kind of delulu.

• 'Am I being delulu?' means 'Am I imagining this?'
• 'Delulu is the solulu' is used to hype a bold, unlikely goal
• Often said about crushes, celebrity fantasies or dream jobs
• Usually self-deprecating and funny, not an insult

• Use it about yourself, playfully: 'Maybe I'm delulu, but I'm applying'
• Avoid calling someone delulu about something they care deeply about; it can sting
• Healthy delulu: big dreams with action
• Unhealthy delulu: ignoring clear evidence and getting hurt

lessons.action: Name one 'delulu' goal you secretly have, and take one small real step toward it.

quiz.q: Where did 'delulu' first become popular?
quiz.why: Fans used it about fantasies involving idols.

quiz.q: What does 'delulu is the solulu' mean?
options: A bit of crazy confidence can be the answer
quiz.why: It playfully celebrates bold belief.

quiz.q: Which is the risky kind of delulu?
options: Ignoring clear signs someone isn't interested
quiz.why: Delusion that ignores reality can lead to hurt.

lessons.title: Rizz
lessons.summary: The word for charm that won Oxford's Word of the Year in 2023.

term.meaning: Slang for charm or the ability to attract someone, especially romantically.

sections.b: Rizz comes from the middle of the word 'charisma' and was popularised by streamer Kai Cenat. Oxford named it Word of the Year in 2023. You can 'have rizz', 'rizz someone up' (flirt with them) or have 'unspoken rizz' (charm without even trying). People also use it loosely for non-romantic charm, like smooth-talking a client. Real rizz isn't about pickup lines; it's confidence, humour and genuinely listening.

In a pitch meeting, Nikhil cracks a joke, remembers the client's daughter's name from last time, and calmly handles a tough question. After the meeting his teammate says, 'Bro, the rizz on you with that client was crazy.' He closed the deal not with tricks but by making the client feel heard.

• 'He's got rizz' = he's charming
• 'Rizz her up' = flirt with her
• 'No rizz' or 'L rizz' = bad at charming people
• 'Unspoken rizz' = attractive or charming without trying

• Use it in casual chats, not formal emails
• Real rizz: eye contact, curiosity, remembering details, making people laugh
• Don't confuse rizz with being pushy; respect a 'no'
• If someone says you have rizz, just say thanks and enjoy it

lessons.action: In your next conversation, ask one follow-up question about something the other person mentioned. That's the most underrated rizz.

quiz.q: Where does 'rizz' come from?
quiz.why: It's a shortened form of charisma.

quiz.q: What does 'unspoken rizz' mean?
quiz.why: It's effortless, non-verbal charm.

quiz.q: Which year did Oxford pick 'rizz' as Word of the Year?
quiz.why: Oxford chose rizz in 2023.

lessons.title: Situationship
lessons.summary: More than friends, less than a relationship, and nobody wants to define it.

term.meaning: A romantic or physical connection without clear labels, commitment or future plans.

sections.b: A situationship is when you talk every day, maybe go on dates, but it's not officially a relationship. There's no 'what are we?' conversation, or there is, and the answer is 'let's not label it.' For some people that's genuinely fine. The trouble starts when one person wants more and the other doesn't, so someone keeps waiting. It's very common in the dating-app era.

Riya and Aditya have been hanging out for 5 months: weekend dinners, daily memes, he met her friends. But when she mentions a family wedding, he says, 'Let's not make it a big thing.' She realises she's in a situationship and has to decide whether she's okay with that.

• No clear label even after months
• Plans are last-minute and rarely long-term
• You're not sure if you can mention them to family or friends
• Avoiding 'what are we?' because you fear the answer

• Ask yourself honestly: do I want more than this?
• If yes, have the 'what are we' talk; clarity is kinder than months of guessing
• If both of you are genuinely fine without labels, that's allowed
• If you keep hoping it'll turn into more with no signs, it may be time to walk away

lessons.action: If you're in any undefined situation (dating or even a work arrangement), write down what you actually want from it.

quiz.q: A situationship is...
options: A connection without clear labels or commitment
quiz.why: It sits between friendship and a relationship.

quiz.q: When does a situationship usually become painful?
options: When one person wants more and the other doesn't
When they live in the same city
quiz.why: Mismatched expectations cause the hurt.

quiz.q: What's the healthiest move if you want more?
options: Have an honest 'what are we' talk
quiz.why: Clarity beats guessing.

lessons.title: Quiet quitting & quiet firing
lessons.summary: Doing just your job, nothing more. And its sneaky mirror image from managers.

term.meaning: Doing only what your job requires, without the unpaid extra effort, while staying employed.

sections.b: Quiet quitting went viral on TikTok in 2022. Despite the name, nobody actually quits: you do your work, but you stop answering emails at 11 pm and stop volunteering for everything. Some call it laziness; others call it healthy boundaries after burnout. Quiet firing is the flip side: a manager slowly pushes someone out by giving no raises, no good projects and no feedback, hoping they'll leave on their own.

Deepak used to work till midnight, hoping for promotion. After being passed over twice, he logs off at 7, does solid work and skips weekend calls. That's quiet quitting. Meanwhile his friend Sana notices her manager stopped inviting her to key meetings and keeps 'forgetting' her appraisal. That might be quiet firing.

• Quiet quitting: doing the role well, but no extras, no after-hours replies
• Quiet firing: being left out of meetings, no growth, delayed appraisals
• Both often start from broken trust or burnout
• Managers sometimes use 'quiet quitting' to label normal boundaries

• If you're quiet quitting, make sure core work is still strong so it's boundaries, not slacking
• Talk to your manager about expectations before you check out completely
• If you suspect quiet firing, ask directly for feedback and document it
• Either way, start updating your resume; both are signs the fit may be ending

lessons.action: Write down which tasks are your actual job and which are 'extra'. Notice if you're doing extra without being recognised.

quiz.q: Does quiet quitting mean resigning?
options: No, you stay but do only what's required
quiz.why: The 'quitting' is from going above and beyond, not from the job.

quiz.q: What is quiet firing?
options: A manager slowly pushing someone out by withholding growth
quiz.why: It's indirect pressure to make someone leave.

quiz.q: If you suspect quiet firing, a good step is...
options: Ask directly for feedback and keep records
Post about it on LinkedIn immediately
quiz.why: Clarity and documentation protect you.

lessons.title: Main character energy
lessons.summary: Living like you're the hero of your own movie, in a good way or a cringey way.

term.meaning: Confidently treating your life like you're the lead of the story.

sections.b: Main character energy is when someone carries themselves like the star of a film: confident, stylish, doing their own thing. It can mean a healthy self-focus: 'I'm going to enjoy my coffee in the rain and not care who's watching.' But 'main character syndrome' is the cringe version: acting like everyone else is a side character in your story, ignoring their needs.

Meghna takes a solo trip to Rishikesh, journals at a cafe, and picks hobbies just because she enjoys them. Her friends say she's giving main character energy. In the same office, a guy who interrupts everyone in meetings and makes every discussion about himself is showing main character syndrome.

• Positive: confidence, self-care, enjoying small moments
• Negative: self-centred, treating others as extras
• Often seen in aesthetic reels: walking with music, solo dates
• 'Main character moment' means a dramatic, movie-like scene in your life

• Use it to do things for yourself, like solo plans and bold choices
• Remember everyone else is the main character in their own story too
• In meetings: be confident, but let others speak
• It's a compliment when said kindly, a dig when said sarcastically

lessons.action: Do one small 'main character' thing today: a solo walk, a nice lunch alone, or wearing that outfit you've been saving.

quiz.q: Healthy main character energy looks like...
quiz.why: It's about self-confidence, not self-centredness.

quiz.q: What is 'main character syndrome'?
options: Acting like others are just side characters
quiz.why: It's the self-centred version.

quiz.q: 'That was such a main character moment' usually means...
quiz.why: A moment that feels like a film scene.

lessons.title: The ick
lessons.summary: That sudden, sometimes tiny thing that makes you lose attraction instantly.

term.meaning: A sudden feeling of turn-off toward someone, often triggered by a small, unexpected behaviour.

sections.b: You like someone, everything's great, and then they do something small, like chew loudly, call the waiter 'boss' in a rude tone, or run after a ball awkwardly, and suddenly you feel 'eww'. That's the ick. The term has floated around since at least the late 1990s, got a big boost from the UK reality show Love Island, and TikTok made it huge. Some icks are real red flags (being rude to staff); others are just random and harmless (wearing socks with sandals).

Shreya is enjoying a date with Varun until he snaps at the waiter for being slow. She gets the ick, and honestly, that's a fair one. Her friend gets the ick because her date said 'yummy' about food. That one is probably just random.

• 'I got the ick' = I suddenly lost attraction
• 'That's an ick' = that behaviour is a turn-off
• Often small, funny or oddly specific
• Can be playful or genuinely about values (rudeness, arrogance)

• Ask: is this ick about values or just a quirk?
• Value icks (rudeness, dishonesty) are worth taking seriously
• Quirk icks might fade if you like the person; give it a chance
• Don't shame people publicly for harmless icks

lessons.action: Think of one 'ick' you've had and decide: was it a value issue or just a quirk?

quiz.q: What is 'the ick'?
options: A sudden turn-off from a small behaviour
quiz.why: It's an abrupt drop in attraction.

quiz.q: Which ick is most worth taking seriously?
quiz.why: Rudeness reflects values; the others are quirks.

quiz.q: If an ick is just a harmless quirk, you might...
options: Give it time; it may fade
quiz.why: Harmless quirks often stop bothering you once you know someone.

lessons.title: Red, green & beige flags
lessons.summary: Warning signs, good signs and the oddly specific boring-but-harmless signs.

term.meaning: Red flag = warning sign; green flag = good sign; beige flag = neutral, quirky or slightly boring trait.

sections.b: A red flag is a warning: someone who lies, controls who you talk to, or explodes in anger. A green flag is a sign of a healthy person: they apologise, respect your time, celebrate your wins. Beige flag is newer TikTok slang for something neither good nor bad, just a bit odd or bland, like someone who only ever orders dal makhani or names their Wi-Fi after their dog. The terms are used for dates, friends, bosses and even companies.

In an interview, Amit asks about work hours. The manager says, 'We're a family here, we don't count hours.' Red flag. Another company shares a clear leave policy and says they avoid weekend calls. Green flag. The third interviewer has a desk full of identical blue pens and nothing else. Beige flag.

• Red: disrespect, lying, controlling behaviour, 'we're a family' with no boundaries
• Green: consistency, honesty, apologising, respecting a 'no'
• Beige: harmless quirks, routines, very specific habits
• Often used as 'Is this a red flag?' to ask for opinions

• Take red flags seriously, especially if you notice more than one
• Look for green flags as much as red; they tell you what to keep
• Don't overreact to beige flags; they're just personality
• In job interviews, ask questions that reveal flags: 'What does a typical week look like?'

lessons.action: List one green flag in a person or workplace in your life, and tell them you appreciate it.

quiz.q: What is a beige flag?
quiz.why: It's neither good nor bad, just a bit odd or bland.

quiz.q: 'We're a family here, we don't count hours' is usually a...
quiz.why: It often signals poor boundaries and overwork.

quiz.q: Which is a green flag?
options: They cancel plans last minute often
quiz.why: Owning mistakes is a sign of a healthy person.

lessons.title: Ghosting, orbiting & soft ghosting
lessons.summary: Disappearing, watching from afar, and fading out with a 'like'.

term.meaning: Suddenly cutting off all contact with someone without explanation.

sections.b: Ghosting is when someone you were talking to just vanishes: no texts, no calls, no reason. Orbiting is when they stop talking to you but still watch your stories and like your posts, hovering around like a satellite. Soft ghosting is a gentler fade: they reply with just a 'like' or a reaction, never a real conversation. Recruiters and companies ghost too, like when you never hear back after a final interview.

After three dates, Ritu's match stops replying. That's ghosting. Two weeks later, he's watching every Instagram story she posts. That's orbiting. Meanwhile, a recruiter who said 'we'll get back by Friday' never does. Corporate ghosting.

• Ghosting: sudden total silence
• Orbiting: no talk, but story views and likes
• Soft ghosting: reacting to messages with an emoji but never replying
• Corporate ghosting: no update after interviews or offers

• If you're ghosted, it's usually about their avoidance, not your worth
• Send one closure message if you want ('Hey, seems like you're busy, all the best'), then move on
• If you're the one leaving, a short honest message is kinder than vanishing
• For recruiters: follow up once after a week; if silent, move on

lessons.action: If you've been leaving someone on 'seen', send them a short, honest reply today, even if it's 'I can't continue this, but thanks.'

quiz.q: What is orbiting?
options: Not talking but still watching your stories
quiz.why: They hover around your social media without talking.

quiz.q: Soft ghosting looks like...
options: Reacting with a 'like' but never really replying
quiz.why: It's a slow fade using minimal responses.

quiz.q: A kind way to end things instead of ghosting is...
quiz.why: A brief, clear message gives closure.

lessons.title: Gatekeeping
lessons.summary: Once about who gets in, now also about not sharing your secret cafe.

term.meaning: Controlling access to something; in slang, refusing to share a good find so it stays exclusive.

sections.b: The original meaning is about power: gatekeepers like editors, HR or senior people decide who gets access to jobs, opportunities or communities. 'Gatekeeping' in that sense is when people unfairly block others, like a senior who says 'you're not a real developer unless you use Vim.' The newer internet slang is lighter: refusing to share where you bought your kurta or which cafe has the best filter coffee, so it doesn't get crowded. 'Stop gatekeeping!' basically means 'just tell us!'

On Instagram, Pallavi posts a gorgeous saree, and comments flood in: 'Don't gatekeep, where's it from?' That's the slang sense. At work, her team lead won't let juniors attend client calls, saying they 'aren't ready'. That's the original sense, and it can hold careers back.

• Slang: 'Gatekeeping my favourite cafe', 'Don't gatekeep the skincare'
• Original: people blocking access to jobs, communities or knowledge
• Hobby gatekeeping: 'You're not a real fan if you don't know X'
• 'Ungatekeeping' or 'I'm not gatekeeping' = sharing a good find

• Slang sense is mostly harmless; share if you want, keep it if you want
• Original sense: watch out if someone blocks your growth unfairly
• If you're senior, open doors: invite juniors, share knowledge
• When people gatekeep hobbies, ignore them and keep enjoying it

lessons.action: Share one useful resource (a course, a tool, a tip) with a junior or friend today. Ungatekeep it.

quiz.q: What is the original meaning of gatekeeping?
options: Controlling who gets access to opportunities
quiz.why: It's about power over access.

quiz.q: 'Don't gatekeep, where's that from?' means...
quiz.why: The slang sense is about sharing a find.

quiz.q: A senior who won't let juniors join client calls is showing...
quiz.why: Blocking access to growth is the original meaning.

lessons.title: Soft launch & hard launch
lessons.summary: Hinting at a new partner online versus the full reveal.

term.meaning: Subtly hinting at something new, often a relationship, before officially announcing it.

sections.b: These terms came from business (a soft launch is a quiet release to test a product) and moved into dating slang. A relationship soft launch is a hint: two coffee cups on an Instagram story, someone's hand in a photo, a mystery shoulder. A hard launch is the full reveal: faces, names, maybe a caption with a heart. People also use these terms for job changes, side projects or anything they're ready to share in stages.

Ankit posts a story of two plates at a restaurant. His friends DM, 'Who is she??' That's the soft launch. Months later, he posts a clear photo with his partner at a wedding, tagged, with 'my person'. Hard launch complete. At work, his company soft-launches a new app to 500 users first.

• Soft launch: blurry photos, hands, two drinks, no names
• Hard launch: face, name, tag, official caption
• Business soft launch: limited, quiet release to test
• 'Hard launching my new job' = officially announcing it on LinkedIn

• Soft launching is a fine way to keep things private early on
• Make sure your partner is okay before any launch
• For products: soft launch to test, then hard launch with full marketing
• Don't over-read soft launches; sometimes two cups is just two cups

lessons.action: Think of a side project or goal you could 'soft launch', like telling one or two friends, before going public.

quiz.q: A relationship soft launch is...
options: Subtly hinting at a partner without revealing them
quiz.why: It's a teaser, not a full reveal.

quiz.q: Where did 'soft launch' originally come from?
quiz.why: Businesses quietly released products to test them first.

quiz.q: Which is a hard launch?
options: A tagged photo with partner's face and name
A mystery hand on a steering wheel
A photo of two coffee cups
quiz.why: A hard launch is the full, clear reveal.

lessons.title: Touch grass
lessons.summary: A cheeky way of saying: log off and go outside.

term.meaning: Slang telling someone they're too online and should go outside and reconnect with real life.

sections.b: 'Touch grass' started in gaming and online forums. If someone's ranting too hard about a minor internet drama, someone else replies 'go touch grass'. It's usually a light roast, but it has a real point: spending time outside and offline is linked in research to better mood and less stress. These days people even say it about themselves: 'I need to touch grass this weekend.'

Karthik has spent three hours arguing with strangers in a Twitter thread about which IT company has the worst appraisal system. His friend messages, 'Bro, touch grass.' He laughs, closes the app, and goes for a walk around Cubbon Park. He feels much better.

• Said when someone is too invested in online fights
• Used to tease people who seem out of touch with real life
• People say it about themselves after a long screen streak
• Can sound rude if said to someone who's genuinely upset

• Take it as a nudge, not an insult; a short walk really does help
• Use it with friends who'll get the joke, not in serious discussions
• Plan offline time: a weekend trek, a walk without your phone
• Notice when online arguments are eating your mood

lessons.action: Go outside for 10 minutes today without your phone. Literally touch some grass if you can.

quiz.q: 'Touch grass' usually means...
options: Log off and reconnect with real life
quiz.why: It's a nudge to go offline.

quiz.q: Where did the phrase start?
quiz.why: It began as an online roast.

quiz.q: When can saying 'touch grass' come off as rude?
options: When said to someone genuinely upset
When you go for a walk
quiz.why: It dismisses real feelings if used at the wrong time.

lessons.title: Brain rot
lessons.summary: Oxford's 2024 Word of the Year, for the mush your brain feels after endless scrolling.

term.meaning: The feeling of mental fog or dullness from consuming too much low-quality online content.

sections.b: Brain rot was named Oxford Word of the Year 2024. It describes that zombie feeling after two hours of reels, and also the silly, meme-heavy content that causes it (like 'skibidi toilet'). Fun fact: the phrase isn't new; it appears in Henry David Thoreau's book 'Walden' from 1854. It's not a medical diagnosis; it's a way of describing how endless low-effort content can leave you tired, distracted and unable to focus.

Neha opens Instagram 'for 5 minutes' at 11 pm and looks up at 1 am. The next day, she can't focus in her standup and keeps reaching for her phone. 'My brain is rotting,' she jokes. That's brain rot in action.

• Losing track of time while scrolling
• Struggling to read a long article or watch a full movie
• Speaking in memes and inside jokes from reels
• Feeling tired and empty after hours of content

• Set app timers; even 30-minute limits help
• Swap one scroll session for something with depth: a book chapter, a podcast, a walk
• Keep your phone out of the bedroom at night
• Don't feel guilty about fun content; just balance it

lessons.action: Set a daily time limit on your most-used social app today.

quiz.q: Which year was 'brain rot' Oxford's Word of the Year?
quiz.why: Oxford chose brain rot in 2024.

quiz.q: Where does the phrase first appear?
quiz.why: Thoreau used it in 1854.

quiz.q: Is brain rot a medical diagnosis?
quiz.why: It's slang, not a medical term.

lessons.title: Boundaries
lessons.summary: Healthy limits that protect you, and how the word can be misused.

term.meaning: Limits you set on what you will accept or do, to protect your time, energy and wellbeing.

sections.b: A healthy boundary is about your own behaviour: 'I don't reply to work messages after 9 pm' or 'I'll leave if you shout at me.' It tells people what you'll do, not what they must do. The word has become trendy, and sometimes people use it as control: 'My boundary is that you can't talk to your friends.' That's not a boundary; that's a rule on someone else's life. Real boundaries are about protecting yourself, not controlling others.

Anjali tells her manager, 'I'm offline after 8, but if there's an emergency, call me.' That's a healthy boundary. Her cousin's boyfriend says, 'My boundary is you can't go out without me.' That's control dressed up as a boundary.

• Healthy: 'I will...' or 'I won't...' statements about yourself
• Unhealthy: 'You can't...' rules on someone else's choices
• Boundaries are enforced by your actions, not by punishing others
• Respecting other people's boundaries matters just as much as having your own

• Phrase it simply: 'I'm not available for calls after 9, but I'll reply first thing in the morning'
• Be consistent; a boundary you don't keep isn't a boundary
• Expect pushback at first; that's normal
• If someone's 'boundary' is controlling your life, that's a red flag

lessons.action: Pick one small boundary (like no email on Sunday mornings) and say it clearly to one person this week.

quiz.q: Which is a healthy boundary?
options: You can't talk to your friends
I don't reply to work messages after 9 pm
You must check in every hour
quiz.why: It's about your own behaviour.

quiz.q: How are boundaries enforced?
quiz.why: You enforce a boundary by what you do.

quiz.q: When does 'boundary' become control?
options: When it's about your own time
When you set it at work
When it dictates someone else's choices
quiz.why: Rules on others' lives are control, not boundaries.

lessons.title: Bare minimum Monday & lazy girl job
lessons.summary: Two TikTok trends pushing back against hustle culture.

term.meaning: Easing into the week by doing only essential tasks on Monday to reduce stress.

sections.b: Bare minimum Monday was popularised by TikToker Marisa Jo Mayes around 2022-23. Instead of starting the week in panic mode, you spend Monday morning on self-care and only the must-do tasks. Lazy girl job, coined by Gabrielle Judge in 2023, means a job that's low-stress, decently paid, often remote, with good work-life balance. Despite the names, neither is about being lazy; both are pushbacks against burnout and hustle culture.

Rohit dreads Mondays, so he tries a bare minimum Monday: no meetings before 11, a slow breakfast, then just the key emails and one important task. By Tuesday he's more energetic. His cousin moves from a startup with 70-hour weeks to a stable 9-to-6 role with good pay. She proudly calls it her lazy girl job.

• Bare minimum Monday: light, essential-only Monday
• Lazy girl job: low-stress, decent pay, good balance
• Both are reactions to burnout and hustle culture
• Critics say the names make them sound lazy; supporters say it's healthy

• If you try bare minimum Monday, still do your critical tasks so no one is blocked
• Talk to your manager if you need a lighter Monday start
• A 'lazy girl job' can be a smart choice, especially when you value time over titles
• Rest is productive; but make sure the trade-offs (growth, pay) fit your goals

lessons.action: Plan next Monday: pick 3 essential tasks only, and move everything else to Tuesday or later.

quiz.q: What is bare minimum Monday?
options: Doing only essential tasks on Monday to ease stress
quiz.why: It's about a gentler start to the week.

quiz.q: A 'lazy girl job' is...
options: A low-stress job with decent pay and balance
quiz.why: It's about balance, not actual laziness.

quiz.q: Both trends are reactions to...
quiz.why: They push back against always-on work culture.

lessons.title: FOMO, JOMO & FOBO
lessons.summary: Fear of missing out, joy of missing out, and fear of better options.

term.meaning: Fear of missing out: the anxiety that others are having fun or opportunities without you.

sections.b: FOMO is that feeling when you see friends' Goa trip reels and feel left out, or everyone's buying a stock and you panic-buy too. The term was popularised by Patrick McGinnis in the early 2000s. JOMO, the joy of missing out, is the opposite: happily skipping things and enjoying your own quiet time. FOBO, fear of better options, is when you can't commit to anything because something better might come along, like refusing a good job offer in case a dream offer appears. (FOBO is also sometimes used for 'fear of becoming obsolete', like worrying AI will replace your job.)

Shruti sees colleagues buying crypto and invests in panic. That's FOMO, and it usually ends badly. Her friend skips a big party to read and sleep early, and feels great. That's JOMO. Their roommate has been 'deciding' between three flats for two months and lost all three. That's FOBO.

• FOMO: checking social media constantly, panic decisions, saying yes to everything
• JOMO: enjoying downtime, no guilt about skipping plans
• FOBO: endless comparing, delaying decisions, keeping all options open
• FOMO and FOBO are often triggered by social media

• For FOMO: pause before acting; ask 'Would I want this if no one else was doing it?'
• For JOMO: plan intentional 'off' time and enjoy it
• For FOBO: set a deadline and 2 or 3 must-have criteria, then pick the first option that meets them
• Remember: you'll always miss something, and that's normal

lessons.action: Skip one plan or app session this week on purpose, and notice whether you feel FOMO or JOMO.

quiz.q: What does FOBO usually mean?
quiz.why: It's the fear that something better might come along.

quiz.q: JOMO is...
quiz.why: It's enjoying skipping things.

quiz.q: A good fix for FOBO is...
options: Set a deadline and clear criteria, then decide
quiz.why: Deadlines and criteria break decision paralysis.
